The transfer is subject to the Government’s decision under the ‘Golden Power’ procedure and the competition authority’s approval, both of which have yet to rule on the transaction, as well as other regulatory requirements. text:
Delta Air Lines, alongside industry partners and public officials, has marked the opening of a new sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) blending facility in Minnesota, providing supply to Minneapolis–St. Paul International Airport (MSP).

Located at Flint Hills Resources’ Pine Bend Refinery, the facility is designed to blend up to 30 million gallons of neat SAF each year with conventional jet fuel before it is transported to the airport using existing pipeline infrastructure.

Minneapolis–St. Paul is Delta’s second-largest hub, where the airline uses approximately 250 million gallons of jet fuel annually.

The project forms part of the Minnesota SAF Hub, a coalition established in 2023 by Delta Air Lines, Greater MSP Partnership, Bank of America, Ecolab and Xcel Energy to support the development of a regional sustainable aviation fuel industry. Plans for the blending facility were first announced in September 2024.

The opening ceremony was attended by representatives from Delta, Flint Hills Resources, Ecolab and Greater MSP, alongside federal and state officials including US Senator Amy Klobuchar, Minnesota Governor Tim Walz and Congressman Brad Finstad.

Peter Carter, President of Delta Air Lines, said:

This facility is the culmination of a shared vision for Minnesota to become a leader in sustainable aviation fuel. By expanding the infrastructure needed to support broader SAF adoption, it represents an important step toward turning that potential into reality. Delta is proud to be part of this effort and excited about the role Minnesota can play in advancing the future of sustainable aviation fuel.

Sustainable aviation fuel is produced from renewable feedstocks and can be blended with conventional jet fuel for use in existing aircraft engines. It is intended to reduce lifecycle carbon emissions compared with conventional aviation fuel without requiring changes to current airport fuelling infrastructure.

title: Commission plan to extend ETS scheme beyond Europe draws international fire
description:
Critics argue move to apply ETS on flights from Europe to neighbouring countries from 2029 is ‘extraterritorial’ and rally behind CORSIA.
“Expanding the EU ETS for aviation would introduce the potential for double charging for CO₂ emissions from international aviation, with implications for the effective implementation of CORSIA,” it says.
“The proposal also risks fragmenting global aviation decarbonisation efforts and jeopardising the achievement of ICAO’s collective global aspirational goals for the international aviation sector.
“AAPA believes that a unilateral, regional extension of EU ETS risks setting a precedent for fragmented, extraterritorial climate measures that could undermine this multilateral framework over time,” it says.
“For the first time ever, international flights are regulated by the EU.
text:
Critics argue move to apply ETS on flights from Europe to neighbouring countries from 2029 is ‘extraterritorial’ and rally behind CORSIA.

While the European Commission’s recent proposals on expanding the scope of its Emissions Trading System (ETS) beyond the European Economic Area appeared, in part, designed to limit the extent to which Europe was set back on a collision course with other territories and stakeholders, it has garnered frustrated responses from across the spectrum.

That, perhaps, was impossible to avoid given the almost diametrically opposed positions of industry and environmental groups in terms of the extent and way in which tax should be used to tackle aviation emissions and on the future growth of the sector.

But it also reflects Europe once again promoting a unilateral approach to addressing aviation emissions, rather than through the global carbon offsetting and reduction scheme for international aviation (CORSIA) agreed at ICAO more than a decade ago and which first put implementation of EU ETS on international flights on hold.

The Commission’s proposals form part of a wider review of the EU ETS scheme and come after its own assessment of the progress of CORSIA implementation judged the latter has not been “sufficiently strengthened yet” as it represents less than 70% of international aviation emissions.

Under the proposals outlined on 17 July, the Commission suggests expanding the ETS to cover flights outside of the European Economic Area, Switzerland and Gibraltar for the first time. Significantly, however, this is being extended to the neighbourhood of the EU, rather than all services into Europe, by only applying to flights 5,000km (3,107mi) from the geographic centre of the European Union.

It also comes with a package of measures aimed at boosting sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), extending allowances, avoiding double-counting with CORSIA, and will only take effect from 2029 – effectively a further two-year extension to the existing ‘stop the clock’ legislation, which has been in place since 2012 when the Commission first paused the application of its ETS to flights outside of Europe.

Significantly, by extending its application to routes of only up to 5,000km, from effectively Frankfurt, the scheme will not cover transatlantic flights nor services to Asia-Pacific.

This means it will not apply on flights to a number of countries which have so far shown a lukewarm approach to CORSIA. Big aviation markets like Brazil, China and India have not participated in the voluntary stage of CORSIA, though will do so from 2027 when the scheme becomes mandatory for major markets.

It could also avert a potential direct stand-off with the USA. The latter under the then Obama Administration had led international pushback to EU ETS applying to international flights, and there is little reason to think the incumbent Trump Administration would view such a move any more favourably given its ‘America First’ approach and criticism at last year’s ICAO general assembly of states using taxes and charges on airspace as an economic stick.

Middle East impact

However, the proposals will cover flights to parts of Africa, Central Asia and the Middle East. In the latter, it means ETS will apply on flights to major Gulf hubs such as Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Doha and Riyadh – though probably not Muscat in Oman, which is more than 5,000km from Frankfurt.

Calling the 5,000km boundary “inherently arbitrary”, the Arab Air Carriers Organisation (AACO) says it considers EU measures to be “inconsistent” with the Chicago Conversion, which it notes “recognises the sovereignty of each state over its airspace, and that no state has the right to impose regulations beyond its territory”.

It adds: “It would have no recognised legal basis, environmental threshold or internationally agreed methodology. It would be selected unilaterally, without the agreement of the affected third states, and would impose different obligations on otherwise comparable routes solely because of a chosen distance threshold.”

AACO also argues the extension of ETS risks undermining ongoing global efforts through CORSIA.

“CORSIA was developed within ICAO, with the agreement of EU member states, as the only global framework for addressing emissions from international aviation,” it says.

“The EU proposal would disrupt those global efforts and significantly increase airline operational complexity and costs, which would ultimately raise the cost of air travel, particularly travel from Europe.”

For its part, ICAO also expressed concern that the measures would undermine CORSIA and result in duplicative measures.

“Expanding the EU ETS for aviation would introduce the potential for double charging for CO₂ emissions from international aviation, with implications for the effective implementation of CORSIA,” it says.

“The proposal also risks fragmenting global aviation decarbonisation efforts and jeopardising the achievement of ICAO’s collective global aspirational goals for the international aviation sector.

“These concerns were highlighted at the 42nd Session of the ICAO Assembly in 2025, where member states unanimously provided ICAO with a clear and reinforced mandate to advance its environmental protection agenda.

“This includes advancing CORSIA, which was designed to give aviation the certainty needed to move forward on its path to net-zero carbon emissions by delivering direct environmental benefits and by ensuring a level playing field, transparency and cost-effectiveness.”

While limiting the scope of the extension of ETS means the scheme will not apply to fights to Asia-Pacific – a move welcomed by the Association of Asia-Pacific Airlines (AAPA) – the latter still echoed ICAO’s concerns.

“AAPA believes that a unilateral, regional extension of EU ETS risks setting a precedent for fragmented, extraterritorial climate measures that could undermine this multilateral framework over time,” it says.

“We encourage the European Parliament, Council and Commission, as this proposal is negotiated in the months ahead, to reaffirm their support for CORSIA and the integrity of the global, consensus-based approach it represents.”

Likewise, US carrier industry group, Airlines for Americas (A4A), also criticised the extraterritorial approach.

“This proposal does make improvements in the use of revenues from EU ETS, but extending the scope to international flights outside of the European region violates international agreements and reopens a contentious chapter in international aviation on environment matters,” it says.

The Commission’s proposal has also riled environmental groups. Transport & Environment, for instance, describes it as “half-hearted” and calls for it to go further.

“For the first time ever, international flights are regulated by the EU. But, due to industry pressure, only a proportion of journeys will be covered, and the longest, most polluting flights will remain exempt,” says T&E aviation director Diane Vitry.

“This must only be a starting point. The ball is now in the member states’ court. They must, at the very least, support this commitment while pushing to gradually expand the coverage before the next review.”

Europe to review CORSIA again

Europe appeared to give itself further leeway, not just by delaying the implementation of of its ETS extension until 2029, but also by putting in place a further review of CORSIA in 2032.

It says in the event CORSIA “is proving to be ambitious, efficient and successful”, the scope of effective carbon pricing under the EU ETS should be reduced to flights within the EEA and departing to the UK, Switzerland and Gibraltar.

But it adds: “If CORSIA still does not deliver by then, the Commission may consider extending the scope to full departing flights.”

text:
The Australian government has committed $32 million to support the development of a project that will convert forestry residues into sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), as part of efforts to strengthen domestic fuel security and reduce reliance on imported liquid fuels.

The funding, provided through the Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA), will support HAMR Energy’s project to convert forest waste into renewable methanol, which can then be processed into sustainable aviation fuel, renewable diesel and other low-carbon liquid fuels, Australian Flying reported.

ARENA will provide the funding in two phases, with $12.5 million allocated for the Front End Engineering Design (FEED) stage and a further $19.5 million available once the company secures co-funding for the detailed engineering phase.

The project, with a total estimated cost of $92 million, will prepare three facilities for future investment decisions. These include a biomass processing plant in Victoria capable of handling around 600,000 tonnes of forestry residues annually, the Portland Renewable Fuels facility that will produce about 300,000 tonnes of renewable methanol each year, and a Methanol-to-Jet plant in Gillman, South Australia, designed to manufacture around 140 megalitres of sustainable aviation fuel annually.

The feedstock will consist of forestry residues such as sawdust, bark, woodchips and thinning material left after timber harvesting. These by-products currently have limited commercial value, offering plantation owners an additional revenue stream while supporting renewable fuel production.

The Australian government said the project would help reduce emissions from the aviation sector, where sustainable aviation fuel is regarded as one of the most practical options for decarbonising long-haul flights.

Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen said Australia has abundant forestry residues that can be converted into clean fuels for difficult-to-decarbonise sectors such as aviation.

He said the project would reduce emissions while supporting regional employment and industrial development.

Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development and Local Government Minister Catherine King said producing low-carbon fuels in South Australia and Victoria would create opportunities across the forestry, manufacturing, engineering and aviation sectors. She added that the investment forms part of the government’s Low Carbon Liquid Fuels Innovation Fund.

South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas said the project would help establish a domestic jet fuel industry and reduce Australia’s long-term dependence on imported liquid fuels, strengthening the country’s energy security.

text:
Delta Expands SAF Infrastructure at Minneapolis-St. Paul Airport

Delta Air Lines has joined partners from the Minnesota SAF Hub, along with federal and state officials, to mark the opening of a new sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) blending facility at Flint Hills Resources’ Pine Bend Refinery. The facility is expected to increase the availability of SAF for flights operating from Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport (MSP).

The new facility enables sustainable aviation fuel to be blended locally with conventional jet fuel before being transported through the existing pipeline network to MSP. Delta uses around 250 million gallons of jet fuel each year at the airport.

The blending facility is designed to process up to 30 million gallons of neat SAF annually, supporting the infrastructure required to increase the use of sustainable aviation fuel in airline operations.

Delta and Flint Hills Resources first announced plans for the project in September 2024. The facility is one of four initiatives identified by the Minnesota SAF Hub, a coalition formed in 2023 by Delta, Greater MSP Partnership, Bank of America, Ecolab and Xcel Energy to support the development of a regional sustainable aviation fuel industry.

Representatives from Delta, Flint Hills Resources, Ecolab, Greater MSP Partnership and state and federal government attended the opening ceremony, including Delta President Peter Carter, Minnesota Governor Tim Walz and U.S. Senator Amy Klobuchar.

Peter Carter said the facility reflects a shared effort to expand sustainable aviation fuel infrastructure in Minnesota and support wider adoption of SAF across the aviation sector.

Sustainable aviation fuel is produced from renewable feedstocks and can reduce lifecycle carbon emissions compared with conventional jet fuel. It can also be transported through much of the existing fuel infrastructure already used by airports. However, limited production remains one of the main challenges to increasing its use across the aviation industry.

The new facility supports Delta’s wider sustainable aviation fuel strategy, including its recently announced five-year collaboration with Shell Aviation to increase SAF availability across key airports in the United States through 2030.

The airline has set a target for 10% of its jet fuel consumption to come from sustainable aviation fuel by 2030 as part of its broader goal of reaching net zero carbon emissions by 2050.

Sustainable Aviation Fuel: Production Routes and Specifications SAF represents a range of certified production pathways aimed at creating aviation-grade hydrocarbons from renewable sources.
Lignocellulosic Biomass Valorization for Sustainable Aviation Fuel Production Lignocellulosic biomass (LCB) has emerged as one of the important renewable carbon platforms for SAF production because of its global abundance, renewable carbon availability, and molecular compatibility with aviation fuel chemistry (Figure 3).
Critically, catalyst acidity, reactant ratios, and thermal conditions govern carbon-chain growth and cycloalkane formation, directly influencing aviation fuel energy density and low-temperature operability.

Abstract

Decarbonizing the aviation sector remains one of the most challenging aspects of the global energy transition because commercial aviation relies on high-energy-density liquid hydrocarbon fuels that cannot be readily replaced by electrification or hydrogen in the near term. Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) has emerged as a viable solution for reducing lifecycle greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions while maintaining compatibility with existing aircraft, engines, and fuel infrastructure. This review presents an assessment of renewable biomass, waste-derived feedstocks, and captured CO2 as sustainable carbon resources for SAF production. This study compares biological, thermochemical, electrochemical, and catalytic routes. Comparative evaluation indicates that no single technology can independently satisfy future aviation fuel demand; instead, integrated, feedstock-flexible circular-carbon biorefineries combining complementary conversion technologies provide the most promising route toward large-scale SAF deployment. Finally, this review identifies key research gaps and commercialization barriers, highlighting feedstock availability, renewable hydrogen integration, standardized sustainability assessment, and integrated biorefinery development as critical priorities for advancing scalable, ASTM-compliant, low-carbon aviation fuels and supporting the transition toward net-zero aviation.

1. Introduction

The global aviation industry is one of the most critical pillars of modern economic development, enabling international trade, tourism, logistics, scientific collaboration, and geopolitical connectivity [1]. However, aviation remains among the most difficult sectors to decarbonize because of its strict energy-density requirements, safety constraints, long-haul operational demands, and reliance on liquid hydrocarbon fuels [2,3]. Currently, aviation contributes approximately 2.5–3% of global anthropogenic greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and nearly 12% of transportation-related carbon emissions, while global jet fuel demand is projected to exceed 500 million tonnes annually by 2050 if no major interventions are implemented. Conventional aviation fuels such as Jet A and Jet A-1 are derived from petroleum refining processes and consist predominantly of C8–C16 paraffins, isoparaffins, cycloalkanes, and aromatics optimized for high gravimetric energy density, low freezing point, thermal stability, and combustion efficiency [4]. Despite continuous improvements in aircraft efficiency and operational optimization, the aviation sector’s growing demand trajectory continues to intensify concerns regarding fossil fuel dependency, climate change, and long-term energy security.

Unlike ground transportation, where electrification is rapidly progressing, full electrification of long-distance aviation remains technologically constrained due to limitations in battery energy density and aircraft weight penalties [5]. Similarly, although hydrogen-powered aviation presents long-term promise, major barriers related to cryogenic storage, infrastructure development, safety, and volumetric energy density continue to hinder immediate deployment. SAF has emerged as the most technologically mature and practically deployable pathway for near- and medium-term aviation decarbonization [6,7,8]. SAFs are considered “drop-in” fuels because they can be integrated into existing aircraft engines, fuel distribution systems, and airport infrastructure without substantial modifications. Importantly, SAFs derived from renewable biomass and waste feedstocks can reduce lifecycle GHG emissions by 50–90% relative to conventional jet fuel while maintaining equivalent aviation performance characteristics [9]. The significant rise in SAF-related publications over the past two decades reflects a growing commitment to SAF technologies and strategies for decarbonizing the aviation industry (Figure 1).

At present, the hydroprocessed ester and fatty acid (HEFA) pathway dominates commercial SAF production and accounts for more than 99% of global SAF output [10,11]. HEFA primarily utilizes lipid-based feedstocks including used cooking oil (UCO), fats, oils, greases (FOGs), animal fats, vegetable oils, and algal lipids [12]. Although HEFA technology is technologically mature and ASTM-certified, the limited availability of sustainable lipid feedstocks, increasing competition with food and cosmetic industries, and concerns regarding indirect land-use change significantly constrain its scalability. Consequently, expanding the renewable carbon pool for SAF production has become a global research priority. In this context, second- and third-generation feedstocks—including lignocellulosic biomass, agricultural residues, forestry waste, municipal solid waste (MSW), food waste, wastewater sludge, volatile fatty acids (VFAs), spent coffee grounds, pyrolysis oils, and waste plastics—have emerged as promising alternative carbon sources capable of supporting large-scale SAF deployment while simultaneously advancing circular economy principles [12,13,14,15]. Among renewable feedstocks, lignocellulosic biomass (LCB) represents one of the most abundant and sustainable organic carbon reservoirs on Earth. Agricultural residues such as corn stover, rice husks, wheat straw, sugarcane bagasse, and forestry by-products possess enormous potential for SAF production because they do not directly compete with food production and are widely distributed globally. Agricultural residues and lignocellulosic waste could provide billions of liters of SAF annually, fulfilling 10–20% of aviation demand and promoting waste valorization and a circular bioeconomy [8].

The conversion of lignocellulosic biomass into aviation-grade hydrocarbons employs thermochemical, biochemical, and catalytic methods. Key thermochemical processes include gasification/Fischer–Tropsch (FT) synthesis, pyrolysis, and hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL), which transform biomass into syngas, bio-oils, and biocrudes [15]. FT synthesis stands out for producing high-quality synthetic paraffinic kerosene (SPK) with superior thermal stability and combustion properties. Additionally, fast pyrolysis, when paired with hydrodeoxygenation (HDO) and hydrocracking, shows significant promise for generating aviation-range hydrocarbons from bio-oils derived from agricultural waste, enhancing the sustainability of aviation fuels [16]. Biochemical conversion routes, particularly anaerobic fermentation and arrested methanogenesis, have garnered significant attention for their potential in sustainable fuel production. Organic wastes—such as food waste, wastewater sludge, and animal manure—can be transformed into volatile fatty acids (VFAs), which are crucial intermediates for producing jet-fuel-range hydrocarbons [12]. Advanced membrane-assisted anaerobic digestion systems enhance carbon redirection towards butyrate- and acetate-rich VFAs while minimizing methane emissions. The catalytic ketonization of these VFAs, using industrial oxides like ZrO2, yields aviation-relevant ketones, such as 6-undecanone, which can be further processed into n-alkanes for SAF blending [17,18]. Catalyst engineering is integral to the advancements in SAF production, influencing selectivity, carbon retention, fuel quality, and process economics. The development of advanced bifunctional catalysts that combine acidic, metallic, mesoporous, and redox-active sites has demonstrated exceptional effectiveness across various reactions, including hydrodeoxygenation and hydrocracking [19]. Key catalysts such as Co/H-ZSM-22, Ni/ZSM-22, Pd/CeZrOx, Pt/Al2O3, Nb2O5, CoMo/Al2O3, Ni-Mo/Al2O3, H-MCM-22, and Al-SBA-15 enable the selective generation of paraffins, isoparaffins, cycloalkanes, and aromatics, essential for achieving optimal aviation fuel properties. Furthermore, innovations in nanoscale catalyst-interface engineering, particularly through atomic layer deposition (ALD) of TiO2 onto Pt catalysts, have shown that oxygen-vacancy-rich interfaces can enhance n-alkane selectivity significantly while minimizing precious metal usage, underscoring the transformative potential of atomic-scale catalyst design in SAF development [19,20,21]. Waste valorization through catalytic upgrading has broadened SAF feedstock options beyond biomass, incorporating waste plastics, municipal solid waste, tire pyrolysis oils, and hydrothermal liquefaction biocrudes as renewable carbon sources. Notably, the thermochemical upgrading of waste polypropylene via catalytic oligomerization and hydrogenation yields aviation-grade hydrocarbons with favorable ASTM properties. Furthermore, hydroprocessing tyre pyrolysis oil produces cycloalkanes and aromatic-rich fuel fractions, highlighting the dual benefit of addressing waste management issues while contributing to aviation decarbonization goals.

Despite significant advancements in SAF technology, challenges persist in achieving widespread commercialization. Key obstacles include feedstock heterogeneity, hydrogen demand, catalyst deactivation, oxygen removal efficiency, carbon losses, and infrastructure limitations, which impede industrial-scale deployment. Currently, global SAF production accounts for less than 1% of total aviation fuel demand, highlighting the urgent necessity for enhanced technology development, supportive policies, and investment in low-carbon fuel systems. International initiatives like ICAO’s CORSIA, the U.S. SAF Grand Challenge, and the EU’s ReFuelEU Aviation aim to accelerate SAF deployment through blending mandates, carbon reduction targets, and sustainability certification frameworks. This review article examines the evolving landscape of SAF production from renewable biomass and waste-derived feedstocks, highlighting the interconnected roles of biological conversion, catalytic upgrading, reactor engineering, feedstock sustainability, lifecycle carbon mitigation, and circular carbon utilization. Integrating advances in anaerobic fermentation, thermochemical conversion, catalyst-interface engineering, hydroprocessing, and systems-level optimization, it proposes a robust framework for scalable, economically viable, and environmentally sustainable SAF technologies supporting aviation decarbonization and net-zero transitions.

Methodology

This review was carried out through a comprehensive literature survey of peer-reviewed articles obtained from Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar. The focus was primarily on studies published between 2015 and 2026, although seminal works prior to this period were included when relevant to the topic. Key search terms encompassed SAF, lignocellulosic biomass, waste-to-jet pathways, Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids (HEFA), Fischer–Tropsch synthesis, Alcohol-to-Jet processes, hydrothermal liquefaction, volatile fatty acids, algae, catalytic systems, life-cycle assessment, and techno-economic evaluations. Publications were meticulously selected based on their scientific rigor, relevance, novelty, and direct contributions to SAF production, sustainability assessments, catalyst advancements, and commercialization efforts. The analysis aimed to critically integrate findings to reveal technological innovations, identify research gaps, and outline future research directions in the field.

2. Alternative Fuels in Aviation

Decarbonizing aviation requires energy carriers that meet high standards for energy density, safety, and operational performance [22]. Key alternatives under consideration include SAF, hydrogen propulsion, battery-electric systems, and synthetic electro fuels. Hydrogen can achieve near-zero carbon emissions but faces challenges such as cryogenic storage and infrastructure needs, hindering widespread adoption [23]. Battery-electric propulsion is limited by low energy density and weight, making it suitable mainly for short-haul flights [24]. Power-to-Liquid (PtL) fuels, produced from renewable electricity and CO2, show promise for decarbonization but depend on affordable renewable energy and efficient carbon capture for commercialization [25]. Among these options, SAFs stand out as the most viable solution, functioning as drop-in fuels compatible with existing aircraft and infrastructure. Derived from renewable biomass and waste carbon, SAFs can significantly reduce lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions while meeting aviation performance standards Tuus, SAFs can serve as a crucial bridge between traditional aviation and future zero-emission flight technologies, positioning it as a pivotal element in the industry’s transition towards sustainability [5].

Sustainable Aviation Fuel: Production Routes and Specifications

SAF represents a range of certified production pathways aimed at creating aviation-grade hydrocarbons from renewable sources. Currently, eight production routes and three co-processing methods are approved under ASTM D7566, allowing SAF to blend with conventional Jet A/Jet A-1 fuels while adhering to ASTM D1655 performance standards. The leading pathway is Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids (HEFA-SPK), which transforms lipid-rich feedstocks, such as used cooking oils and animal fats, into synthetic paraffinic kerosene. Other approved methods include Fischer–Tropsch (FT), Alcohol-to-Jet (ATJ), and Catalytic Hydrothermolysis (CH), among others (Figure 2). Emerging technologies increasingly leverage second-generation feedstocks like agricultural residues and municipal solid waste, enhancing circular carbon utilization and minimizing reliance on food-based resources. SAF production focuses on generating essential hydrocarbon classes—paraffins, isoparaffins, cycloalkanes, and controlled aromatic fractions—that dictate fuel performance attributes such as energy density and combustion stability. Key factors in this process include catalyst design and hydrocarbon selectivity, which are crucial for producing ASTM-compliant fuels that support the aviation industry’s long-term decarbonization goals.

3. Waste to Sustainable Aviation Fuels

Waste-to-SAF production employs a combination of biological, thermochemical, and catalytic upgrading technologies to transform heterogeneous waste carbon into aviation-grade hydrocarbons. The selection of technology is influenced by factors such as feedstock composition, moisture content, and desired fuel characteristics. Biological methods, including anaerobic digestion and acidogenic fermentation, convert organic waste into volatile fatty acids (VFAs) and other intermediates, which are then upgraded through various chemical processes to produce jet-fuel-range hydrocarbons. Thermochemical approaches, such as gasification and pyrolysis, convert waste into syngas or bio-oils, which require catalytic hydroprocessing to enhance fuel stability and energy density. Catalytic upgrading is crucial across all waste-to-SAF pathways, involving processes like hydrodeoxygenation and oligomerization that dictate carbon-chain growth and hydrocarbon selectivity. The effectiveness of these catalysts—determined by properties such as acidity and metal dispersion—affects carbon retention and conversion efficiency. Successful waste-to-SAF production necessitates the integration of efficient carbon recovery, selective catalytic upgrading, and energy optimization to produce fuels that meet ASTM specifications while maximizing carbon efficiency and minimizing lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions. This holistic approach positions waste-to-SAF as a viable solution for SAF production.

3.1. Lignocellulosic Biomass Valorization for Sustainable Aviation Fuel Production

Lignocellulosic biomass (LCB) has emerged as one of the important renewable carbon platforms for SAF production because of its global abundance, renewable carbon availability, and molecular compatibility with aviation fuel chemistry (Figure 3). Composed primarily of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin, LCB represents the largest reservoir of sustainable organic carbon on Earth and includes agricultural residues, forestry by-products, municipal biowaste, paper sludge, spent coffee grounds, and food-processing residues. Unlike lipid-based SAF feedstocks, lignocellulosic resources avoid direct competition with food systems while simultaneously supporting circular bioeconomy principles through waste valorization and carbon recovery. Traditionally, lignin-rich biomass fractions generated from pulp and paper industries have been treated as low-value residues and predominantly combusted for process heat or utilized in low-grade materials such as fiberboards and oriented strand boards [26]. However, harsh pulping conditions generate stable C–C linkages that increase lignin recalcitrance and limit downstream monomer recovery. Consequently, the “lignin-first” biorefinery has emerged as a transformative strategy that selectively extracts, depolymerizes, and stabilizes lignin while preserving cellulose and hemicellulose fractions for integrated fuel and chemical production. Reductive catalytic fractionation (RCF) has become one of the most promising lignin-first approaches because it enables simultaneous lignin solubilization, depolymerization, and stabilization under reductive catalytic environments [27]. During RCF, lignin is converted into refined lignin oil (RLO), a phenolic-rich bio-oil containing substituted C6 aromatic monomers, dimers, and oligomers with average carbon numbers close to aviation fuel aromatics and naphthenes [28]. The relevance of lignin-derived intermediates for SAF production is particularly important because aviation fuels require controlled aromatic and cycloalkane fractions to regulate energy density, freezing point, viscosity and thermal stability [29,30,31]. However, lignin-derived bio-oils exhibit high oxygen content and therefore require catalytic hydrodeoxygenation (HDO) prior to utilization as aviation fuel blendstocks [32]. Recent studies have demonstrated that lignin extracted through RCF possesses superior physicochemical characteristics for HDO upgrading compared with lignins generated from conventional Organosolv processing. Combining RCF with hydrodeoxygenation can enable efficient production of cycloalkanes, naphthenes, and aromatics suitable for aviation applications while improving overall carbon efficiency and reducing refinery severity [27,28]. The effectiveness of RCF strongly depends on catalyst, solvent system, biomass composition, and reaction conditions. Bifunctional catalysts such as Pd/C, Pd/CNx, Ni/C, and Ru/Al2O3 can cleave β-O-4 ether linkages while hydrogenating unstable intermediates, thereby preventing repolymerization and improving monomer stabilization [33]. Furthermore, metal nanoparticle size and dispersion directly govern hydrodeoxygenation selectivity and removal of residual aliphatic hydroxyl groups, ultimately improving fuel stability and hydrocarbon quality [34].

Beyond lignin valorization, the carbohydrate fraction of LCB provides additional SAF precursor routes through biochemical and thermochemical conversion. Zhu, Lingjun et al. (2023) developed a hydrothermal conversion platform integrating dilute H2SO4 hydrolysis with a highly stable resin-derived carbon solid acid catalyst to selectively produce furfural and levulinic acid from corn stover [35]. The system achieved near-complete carbohydrate conversion with furfural and levulinic acid yields of 68.7 mol% and 70.3 mol%, respectively. These intermediates serve as critical platform molecules for downstream synthesis of paraffins, cycloalkanes, and aromatic aviation hydrocarbons. The catalyst’s intrinsic sulfonic acid functionalities, hydrothermal stability, and large-pore architecture significantly reduced humin formation while improving catalytic longevity over 28 cycles. Similarly, Li, Biomass-derived aldehydes and ketones can be selectively upgraded into aviation hydrocarbons through integrated aldol condensation and hydrodeoxy genation [36]. Using bifunctional Ni/Mg–Al-O/AC catalysts, the process coupled base-mediated carbon–carbon bond formation with metal-assisted hydrogenation can generate C7–C14 paraffins and cycloalkanes with approximately 79% condensate yields and 72% alkane selectivity [36]. Critically, catalyst acidity, reactant ratios, and thermal conditions govern carbon-chain growth and cycloalkane formation, directly influencing aviation fuel energy density and low-temperature operability.

The production of high-density cyclic SAF molecules from lignocellulosic intermediates has also advanced significantly. Li, Zhanchao et al. (2021) developed a selective route for transforming biomass-derived cyclopentanone into bi(cyclopentane)-based aviation hydrocarbons through one-pot condensation and hydrodeoxygenation over Pd/C catalysts [37]. The resulting SAF molecules exhibited exceptionally high densities (0.87–0.94 g cm−3), volumetric heating values reaching 41.4 MJ L−1, and freezing points below −80 °C, comparable to advanced aerospace fuels such as JP-10 and RJ-4. These findings demonstrate that lignocellulosic biomass can serve as a platform for synthesizing next-generation high-energy-density cyclic aviation fuels. Integrated lignocellulosic biorefineries can further strengthen SAF feasibility by maximizing carbon utilization across all biomass fractions. Klein, Bruno Colling et al. (2023) proposed a unified biorefinery integrating co-solvent-enhanced lignocellulosic fractionation (CELF), consolidated bioprocessing, and catalytic lignin valorization [38]. Through selective deconstruction of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin streams, the process generated alcohol, esters, adipic acid, and cycloalkane SAF blendstocks while achieving carbon utilization efficiencies exceeding 50%. Copper porous metal oxide catalysts operating in supercritical methanol selectively converted lignin into cyclic hydrocarbons critical for freezing-point control and fuel stability. Importantly, the system achieved SAF production costs as low as $3.15/GGE while significantly reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

Recent studies also demonstrate the importance of unconventional lignocellulosic waste. Acquah, Christopher et al. (2026) developed a circular biorefinery strategy using spent coffee grounds (SCG) as an integrated SAF feedstock [13]. Through alcohol-based solvolytic fractionation with endogenous glycerol–ethanol solvent systems, the process simultaneously recovered carbohydrate-rich solids, lipid-derived oils, and lignin-rich fractions suitable for HEFA, alcohol-to-jet (ATJ), and HDO pathways. The process achieved > 98% glucan retention, >95% delipidification, and >67% delignification while reducing autogenous pressure by 59%. The resulting SAF precursors included fatty acid esters, lignin monomers, paraffinic intermediates, aromatics, and cycloalkane precursors critical for aviation fuel performance. The optimized ethanol/glycerol system further achieved minimum selling prices near $1.43 kg−1, highlighting the economic viability of integrated waste-derived lignocellulosic SAF systems.

Thermochemical valorization of lignocellulosic agricultural waste has similarly shown exceptional promise. Halimi NAN et al. (2025) demonstrated conversion of corn stover into aviation-grade hydrocarbons through fast pyrolysis followed by two-stage hydrotreatment over Ru/C and CoMo/Al catalysts [21]. The process selectively generated paraffins, isoparaffins, cycloalkanes, and controlled aromatic fractions while reducing undesirable oxygenates. Heat integration eliminated external heating demand and reduced cooling utilities by 55%, while lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions decreased by up to 76% relative to fossil jet fuel. Likewise, Lan Kai et al. (2024) developed a circular-carbon pathway utilizing high-ash paper sludge as feedstock [39]. Through deashing, enzymatic hydrolysis, dehydration, aldol condensation, and hydroprocessing, the process generated aviation-range C8–C16 hydrocarbons with lifecycle emissions as low as 5.1–11.1 gCO2eq MJ−1 after ash recycling, representing up to 94% GHG reduction compared to petroleum jet fuel.

Lipid upgrading from lignocellulosic-associated feedstocks has also evolved beyond conventional HEFA. Hebish, Anas Ahmed et al. (2024) demonstrated hydrogen-free catalytic deoxygenation of triglycerides into paraffins, isoparaffins, cycloparaffins, and aromatics using Ni-, Co-, Pd-, and zeolite-supported catalysts [29]. By eliminating the substantial hydrogen demand associated with conventional hydroprocessing, the approach improved economic feasibility while maintaining aviation-grade hydrocarbon selectivity approaching 90%. Similarly, Liu, Junli et al. (2025) introduced ozone-assisted cracking of oleic-acid-rich lipids into nonanoate esters exhibiting ultra-low cloud points (−35 to −67 °C), exceptional oxidation stability, and up to 93% CO2 reduction potential, demonstrating a highly energy-efficient route toward winter-grade SAF molecules [40]. Waste-derived thermochemical systems further broaden lignocellulosic SAF integration. Summers, Sabrina et al. (2025) combined hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL) of food waste with CoMo catalytic hydrotreating to generate ASTM-compliant aviation fuels [31]. The process achieved complete hydrodeoxygenation, near-complete desulfurization, and 87% denitrogenation while preserving carbon and energy recovery efficiencies above 85%. The resulting fuel was rich in n-alkanes, cycloalkanes, isoalkanes, and aromatics essential for combustion stability and freezing-point control.

3.2. Fermentation of Waste: VFA-Based SAF Pathway

Unlike conventional lipid-based SAF systems, fermentation-driven platforms transform heterogeneous wet organic wastes (food waste, municipal biowaste, wastewater sludge, agricultural residues, fats, oils, and greases) into volatile fatty acids (VFAs), alcohols, and oxygenated intermediates that subsequently serve as refinery-compatible SAF precursors (Figure 4). This biological catalytic integration establishes a circular-carbon framework capable of simultaneously reducing landfill methane emissions, valorizing waste streams, and generating aviation-grade hydrocarbons with significantly reduced lifecycle GHG emissions. Fermentation-derived VFA platforms establish a next-generation circular-carbon pathway for SAF, integrating biological waste valorization with advanced catalytic upgrading. By converting heterogeneous wet waste streams into uniform intermediate molecules and subsequently upgrading them into paraffinic, cyclic, and aromatic hydrocarbons, this approach overcomes major limitations associated with feedstock variability and process complexity. A central route within fermentation-connected SAF production is acidogenic/acetogenic fermentation through arrested methanogenesis.

VFAs are key intermediate metabolites formed during anaerobic digestion, where complex organic matter is sequentially degraded by microbial consortia under anaerobic conditions [41]. Under conventional operation, VFAs are rapidly consumed by methanogenic archaea and ultimately converted into methane and carbon dioxide. However, by selectively arresting methanogenesis, the metabolic flux can be redirected from biogas production toward VFA accumulation [42,43]. This is typically achieved by regulating operational parameters such as pH (~5–6), organic loading rate (OLR), hydraulic retention time (HRT), temperature, and substrate availability, thereby suppressing methanogenic activity while maintaining acidogenic and acetogenic microorganisms [44]. Chemical inhibition of methanogenesis provides a highly selective strategy for maximizing VFA accumulation. 2-bromoethanesulfonate (BES/BESA) acts as a structural analogue of coenzyme M, competitively inhibiting methyl-coenzyme M reductase, the terminal and rate-limiting enzyme in methanogenesis that is unique to methanogenic archaea. Similarly, iodopropane functions as a corrinoid antagonist (restricts the functioning of the B12 enzyme which carries methyl group), disrupting methyl-group transfer reactions required for methanogenic metabolism [45,46].

Under methane-suppressed anaerobic conditions, complex organic substrates are biologically converted into short and medium-chain carboxylic acids (C2–C8 VFAs), including acetate, butyrate, valerate, and caproate, Heptanoate and Octanoate [41]. VFAs serve as versatile intermediates for catalytic carbon-chain upgrading, influencing chain elongation, oxygen removal, hydrocarbon structure, and overall fuel quality through established upgrading sequences [47]. The integration of acidogenic/acetogenic fermentation, ketonization, condensation chemistry, cyclization, and hydrodeoxygenation creates a flexible framework for optimizing fuel composition to align with aviation standards [48].

The catalytic ketonization stage is crucial in fermentation-derived SAF systems, influencing carbon-chain growth and hydrocarbon formation. This process effectively produces linear and branched ketones, paraffins, and cycloalkanes that meet the carbon distribution and energy density requirements for aviation fuel [19]. A biocatalytic–thermocatalytic strategy utilizing lignocellulosic biomass can be converted into mixed C2–C8 carboxylic acids via anaerobic fermentation. These acids are then transformed into ethyl esters and upgraded using bifunctional Pd/CeZrOx catalysts, achieving over 90% selectivity for C11+ aviation-range molecules [19]. The catalyst’s multifunctional active sites facilitate various reactions, including ketonization and hydrogenation, within a unified framework. Converting wet waste-derived VFAs into SAF highlights a transformative approach to decarbonizing the aviation sector. Utilizing a sequential catalytic process, VFAs undergo ketonization over ZrO2, cyclization over H/ZSM-5, and hydrodeoxygenation over Pt/Al2O3 to produce aviation-grade hydrocarbons and BTEX compounds. This integrated method not only generates paraffins, cycloalkanes, and aromatics compatible with Jet A specifications but also achieves greenhouse gas reductions compared to traditional fossil jet fuels [49]. Further research by [12] highlighted the potential of VFAs as molecular precursors for SAF. Waste-to-fuel platform combining anaerobic digestion with advanced catalytic processes can yield hydrocarbons that enhance fuel properties such as freezing point and energy density. The ZrO2 catalysts demonstrate significant stability, maintaining activity for over 100 h, while Pt/Al2O3 and Nb2O5 facilitated efficient carbon coupling and oxygen removal. Notably, blending strategies allow for up to 70% renewable fuel content, reducing soot formation by 34% relative to fossil fuels. Lifecycle assessments reveal a substantial greenhouse gas reduction potential of 165%, demonstrating VFA-derived SAF systems as a pivotal solution in the quest for sustainable aviation [12]. Recent advancements in biological conversion technologies have led to the development of membrane-assisted arrested methanogenesis for SAF precursor production [17]. Utilizing submerged membrane bioreactors (SubMBR) combined with resin-wafer electrodeionization (RW-EDI), the process effectively redirects carbon from high-strength wastewater and organic waste into butyrate- and acetate-rich VFAs, achieving concentrations over 113 g/L (Table 1). The optimized production costs for VFAs are $0.60 kg−1, with SAF selling prices at $4.64 GGE−1. Further upgrading through ketonization, aldol condensation, and hydrodeoxygenation yields aviation-grade hydrocarbons with improved freezing points and combustion stability. This approach results in a significant 71% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions compared to fossil Jet A, highlighting its techno-economic and environmental viability. Miller et al., 2022 showed that the ketonization of wet waste-derived VFAs using monoclinic ZrO2 catalysts operates via a Langmuir–Hinshelwood mechanism, where coproduct water acts as a key inhibitor affecting reactor size and efficiency [18]. Implementing staged series-reactor configurations with interstage water removal can reduce reactor size by over 97% while achieving 98% conversion efficiency. The resulting C9–C15 ketones and n-alkanes align with aviation fuel specifications, ensuring optimal freezing point, viscosity, and energy density. Catalyst-interface engineering can improve fermentation-derived SAF. This approach minimizes precious-metal consumption while significantly improving durability and carbon efficiency, highlighting the transformative potential of nanoscale engineering in sustainable fuel production. McNeary W. Wilson et al. (2023) introduced a groundbreaking hydrodeoxygenation method utilizing atomic layer deposition (ALD) to fabricate TiO2-coated Pt/Al2O3 catalysts featuring oxygen-vacancy-rich Pt–TiO2 interfaces [20]. These Ti3+-rich sites significantly boost carbonyl activation, alcohol dehydration, and hydrogen transfer for VFA-derived ketones. The enhanced catalyst achieved complete ketone conversion with 100% selectivity for n-undecane, while increasing n-alkane site-time yield eightfold compared to uncoated variants.

Although VFAs represent a promising intermediate for SAF production, several technical and economic challenges currently limit commercial deployment. First, VFA fermentation typically produces dilute acid streams, making downstream recovery and purification energy-intensive and costly. Conventional separation techniques, including distillation and solvent extraction, often account for a significant fraction of the overall process energy demand, while emerging approaches such as membrane separation, electrodialysis, and reactive extraction require further optimization for industrial application [47]. Second, upgrading VFAs into jet-range hydrocarbons through ketonization, hydrodeoxygenation, oligomerization, or catalytic condensation requires robust catalysts, renewable hydrogen, and efficient carbon management to minimize carbon losses and operating costs. Feedstock variability, process stability, catalyst deactivation, and integration of biological and thermochemical conversion steps remain additional scale-up challenges. Furthermore, comprehensive TEA and LCA studies are still limited, making it difficult to quantify commercial competitiveness relative to established SAF pathways such as HEFA, Fischer–Tropsch, and Alcohol-to-Jet. Future research should therefore prioritize integrated biorefinery designs, intensified product recovery, renewable hydrogen utilization, catalyst development, and pilot-scale demonstrations to improve both economic viability and environmental performance of VFA-derived SAF.

4. Sustainable Aviation Fuel from Algae

Microalgae have emerged as one of the most promising third-generation feedstocks for SAF production because they simultaneously combine carbon capture, wastewater remediation, and renewable fuel synthesis (Figure 5). Unlike terrestrial bioenergy crops, microalgae exhibit high photosynthetic efficiencies, rapid growth rates, elevated lipid accumulation, and the ability to utilize saline water, wastewater, and concentrated industrial CO2 streams without competing for arable land or freshwater resources [54]. A unique advantage of microalgae is their metabolic versatility. They naturally produce triacylglycerols (TAGs), fatty acids, terpenoids, isoprenoids, and hydrocarbon-like molecules that serve as direct SAF precursors [55]. Among these, isoprenoid- and aromatic-derived hydrocarbons are particularly attractive because of their superior energy densities compared to conventional fatty-acid-derived fuels, making them highly suitable for aviation applications [56]. Species such as Botryococcus braunii are especially valuable due to their accumulation of botryococcenes and other hydrocarbon-rich compounds that closely resemble aviation fuel molecules. Currently, the HEFA pathway remains the dominant commercial route for converting algal lipids into aviation fuel. However, feedstock cost represents the major economic bottleneck, accounting for approximately 68–70% of the minimum fuel selling price (MFSP) [57]. Life-cycle assessment indicates that algal-HEFA pathways can achieve carbon intensities of approximately 36 g CO2e MJ−1 SAF, corresponding to nearly 60% lower greenhouse gas emissions than conventional jet fuel, while optimized waste-lipid HEFA systems can reduce emissions by up to 77% [58]. In integrated algal biorefineries, coproduct valorization can reduce production costs, resulting in MFSP values near $4.53 GGE−1. The potential of scalability is substantial. Utilization of point-source CO2 emissions could theoretically generate up to 235 million tonnes of algal biomass annually, corresponding to approximately 59 million tonnes of algal oil production [59]. Under favorable cultivation scenarios, algal oil production costs could decrease from $7–8 gallon−1 to approximately $5–6 gallon−1 when high-value coproducts are included. Consequently, advances in strain development, cultivation efficiency, carbon utilization, and integrated biorefinery concepts will determine the long-term contribution of algal SAF toward achieving global aviation decarbonization targets and the SAF Grand Challenge goal of 35 billion gallons by 2050.

4.1. Hybrid Bio-Thermochemical Pathways

Hybrid bio-thermochemical pathways maximize the value of algal biomass by integrating biological carbon fixation with thermochemical fuel production technologies, including hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL), pyrolysis-to-jet (PTJ), alcohol-to-jet (ATJ), and Fischer–Tropsch synthesis [58]. Unlike conventional HEFA systems that utilize only extracted lipids, these pathways convert the entire algal biomass, substantially improving carbon utilization efficiency and reducing residual waste generation.

Among these technologies, HTL is particularly advantageous because it directly processes wet algal biomass without energy-intensive drying, producing biocrude suitable for subsequent hydroprocessing into aviation-grade hydrocarbons [60]. Recent developments focus on integrating green hydrogen, advanced hydrodeoxygenation catalysts, and refinery co-processing strategies to improve fuel quality while lowering lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions. Co-processing algal biocrudes within existing hydroprocessing units, catalytic crackers, and refinery streams reduces capital investment requirements and accelerates industrial deployment. Consequently, hybrid pathways are increasingly recognized as one of the most commercially realistic routes for converting algal carbon into drop-in SAF while simultaneously improving refinery decarbonization and carbon efficiency.

4.2. Synbio Integration

Synthetic biology is transforming algae from passive biomass producers into programmable biofactories for SAF synthesis. Advanced genetic engineering, metabolic engineering, and CRISPR-based genome editing are being applied to strains including Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, Nannochloropsis spp., Phaeodactylum tricornutum, Chlorella spp., Botryococcus braunii, and Synechocystis to enhance photosynthetic efficiency, carbon fixation, lipid accumulation, and hydrocarbon biosynthesis [61,62]. Particular emphasis is placed on redirecting metabolic flux toward triacylglycerols (TAGs), isoprenoids, and aviation-compatible hydrocarbon precursors while reducing cellular energy losses associated with maintenance metabolism. Organelle-targeted engineering of chloroplasts and endoplasmic reticulum systems further improves conversion of solar energy and CO2 into fuel molecules. Notably, engineered Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 expressing an isoprene synthase gene from Eucalyptus globulus demonstrated direct biosynthesis of isoprene and jet-fuel precursors using only sunlight and carbon dioxide [63]. Design–Build–Test–Learn (DBTL) platforms combined with genome-scale metabolic models are accelerating strain optimization and reducing development cycles, creating next-generation algal biofactories capable of producing aviation fuel precursors with enhanced productivity and lower production costs in carbon-negative synthetic biology [64].

4.3. AI and ML-Based Approaches

Artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and digitalization are transforming algae-based SAF production by enabling intelligent process optimization across the entire cultivation and downstream processing chain [65]. AI-driven platforms integrate Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, computer vision, predictive analytics, and automated control systems to continuously regulate light intensity, nutrient availability, CO2 delivery, temperature, pH, and hydrodynamic conditions, thereby improving process stability and resource utilization [66]. Advanced ML algorithms, including artificial neural networks (ANNs), support vector machines (SVMs), random forests (RF), convolutional neural networks (CNNs), long short-term memory (LSTM) models, XGBoost, and reinforcement learning (RL), have demonstrated high predictive accuracy (R2 values approaching 0.98) for biomass productivity, lipid accumulation, CO2 fixation, and harvesting efficiency, while CNN-based image analysis has achieved approximately 98% accuracy in microalgal species classification [67]. AI-assisted metabolic modelling further supports the identification of genetic targets for enhanced lipid and hydrocarbon biosynthesis, whereas digital twin technologies enable real-time process simulation, contamination detection, predictive maintenance, and energy-efficient operation of large-scale photobioreactors [68,69]. Collectively, these digital technologies improve cultivation efficiency, reduce operational uncertainty, and enhance the economic feasibility and scalability of algae-based SAF production within integrated circular biorefinery systems.

4.4. Carbon Capture and Utilization

Carbon Capture and Utilization (CCU) significantly strengthen the sustainability profile of algal SAF systems by transforming industrial CO2 emissions into productive carbon feedstocks. Flue gases from cement plants, steel industries, thermal power stations, and refineries can be directly utilized to support algal growth, simultaneously reducing emissions and supplying renewable carbon for fuel synthesis. One of the most innovative developments is the Bicarbonate-Based Integrated Carbon Capture and Algae Production System (BICCAPS), where captured CO2 is converted into bicarbonate-rich solutions that serve as transportable and biologically accessible carbon sources for algae and cyanobacteria. Amine-based capture systems employing monoethanolamine, diethanolamine, and triethanolamine further improve bicarbonate generation efficiency [70,71]. BICCAPS offers additional advantages through solvent recycling and coproduct generation, lowering overall carbon mitigation costs [72]. A mixed consortium of Scenedesmus obliquus and Chlorella spp. demonstrated bicarbonate fixation rates of 2.42 g HCO3− per gram of algal biomass, highlighting the strong carbon-capture potential of biological systems [73]. Integration with Bioenergy with Carbon Capture and Storage (BECCS) further expands opportunities for achieving net-negative carbon emissions while supporting sustainable fuel production [74].

4.5. Industrial Flue Gas and Wastewater Systems

Industrial flue gases and wastewater represent low-cost resource streams that can substantially improve the economics and sustainability of algal SAF production. Typical industrial flue gases contain 10–25% CO2 alongside NOx, SOx, fly ash, and particulate matter, creating challenging cultivation conditions that require robust microalgal strains [75]. Thermophilic and acidophilic species such as Viridella and Galdieria exhibit exceptional tolerance to elevated CO2 concentrations and harsh industrial environments, making them attractive candidates for flue-gas-assisted cultivation. Simultaneously, wastewater streams provide water, nitrogen, phosphorus, and trace nutrients necessary for algal growth. Anaerobically digested sewage sludge, municipal wastewater, agricultural effluents, aquaculture discharges, food-processing wastewaters, and landfill leachates have all been successfully utilized for simultaneous phycoremediation and biomass production [76]. Oil and gas industry effluents have also demonstrated potential as cultivation media [77]. Integrating wastewater treatment, nutrient recovery, carbon capture, and algal biomass production within a single system substantially improves resource efficiency while lowering cultivation costs. Consequently, future algal SAF biorefineries are expected to evolve toward fully integrated circular bioeconomy platforms where waste carbon, nutrients, and water are simultaneously recovered and converted into aviation fuel precursors.
