5. From CO2 to SAF: Bioenergy Systems and Renewable Energy Integration

5.1. Biological Routes to SAF

Carbon-neutral liquid fuels synthesized from renewable sources are considered most sustainable and practical long-term strategies for achieving climate-neutral aviation [78,79]. Carbon-to-fuel approaches that integrate bioenergy systems, carbon capture, renewable electricity, and advanced catalytic platforms have recently emerged as highly promising pathways for converting CO2 into SAF [80]. These integrated systems could establish a circular carbon economy in which CO2 from industrial emissions, biomass processing, or direct air capture is recycled into hydrocarbon fuels instead of being directly released into the atmosphere [79]. The approaches simultaneously address greenhouse gas mitigation, renewable energy storage, carbon waste utilization, and sustainable transportation demands [81].

Carbon-to-fuel pathways rely heavily on the integration of renewable carbon sources with advanced thermochemical, biological, and electrochemical conversion technologies [82,83]. Biomass-derived carbon remains one of the most important feedstocks because biomass naturally captures atmospheric CO2 during photosynthesis [84]. Agricultural residues, forestry waste, municipal solid waste, algae, and industrial organic wastes provide renewable carbon resources that can be converted into syngas, bio-oils, alcohols, and hydrocarbon intermediates suitable for aviation fuel synthesis [85]. Gasification technologies convert lignocellulosic biomass into syngas consisting primarily of carbon monoxide and hydrogen, which can subsequently undergo catalytic Fischer–Tropsch synthesis to produce liquid hydrocarbons [86,87]. Similarly, pyrolysis and hydrothermal liquefaction processes generate bio-crude oils that may be upgraded into aviation-grade fuels through hydroprocessing and catalytic refining [5,83]. These bioenergy systems are increasingly integrated with carbon capture technologies to improve carbon utilization efficiency and minimize greenhouse gas emissions throughout the fuel production lifecycle [80].

Carbon capture and utilization (CCU) technologies development has significantly expanded the scope of SAF production beyond traditional biomass feedstocks. Industrial point-source emissions from cement plants, steel manufacturing, power generation facilities, and chemical industries contain concentrated streams of carbon dioxide that can be captured and redirected toward fuel synthesis pathways [88]. Direct air capture technologies are also gaining attention because they enable atmospheric carbon removal independent of industrial infrastructure [89]. Captured carbon dioxide may be combined with renewable hydrogen generated through water electrolysis to synthesize synthetic hydrocarbons through power-to-liquid (PtL) pathways [90]. These systems are particularly attractive because they establish nearly closed carbon cycles when powered entirely by renewable electricity. Renewable hydrogen functions as a key reducing agent during catalytic conversion processes and enables the production of synthetic paraffinic kerosene compatible with existing aviation turbines [91]. The integration of renewable electricity with carbon recycling systems therefore represents a transformative strategy for sustainable aviation decarbonization [92].

Biological carbon conversion systems are attracting considerable scientific interest because they enable CO2 transformation under relatively mild operating conditions. Biological routes utilize microorganisms capable of converting CO2 or syngas into alcohols or hydrocarbons, while electrochemical systems directly reduce CO2 to fuel precursors [93]. Several autotrophic and acetogenic microorganisms naturally possess metabolic pathways capable of fixing carbon dioxide into organic compounds. Cyanobacteria, microalgae, methanogens, and acetogenic bacteria have demonstrated significant potential for converting CO2 or syngas into alcohols, fatty acids, methane, and hydrocarbon precursors relevant to aviation fuel production [93,94]. Among these, acetogenic bacteria operating through the Wood–Ljungdahl pathway are particularly promising because they can utilize both carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide as carbon sources while producing ethanol, acetate, and butanol under anaerobic conditions [95]. Gas fermentation systems employing microorganisms such as Clostridium ljungdahlii and Clostridium autoethanogenum have been extensively investigated for industrial-scale ethanol production from syngas and industrial emissions [96]. The resulting alcohols can subsequently undergo alcohol-to-jet conversion pathways involving dehydration, oligomerization, and hydrogenation to produce aviation-grade hydrocarbons [94,95].

Microalgae-based systems provide another important biological platform for SAF synthesis [97,98]. Algae possess exceptionally high photosynthetic efficiency and can accumulate large quantities of lipids suitable for hydro-processed esters and fatty acids (HEFA) fuel production [99,100]. Unlike terrestrial crops, microalgae cultivation does not necessarily require arable land or freshwater resources, making algal biofuel systems attractive from a sustainability perspective [101]. Algae cultivation can also be integrated with wastewater treatment facilities and industrial carbon emissions to improve nutrient recycling and carbon capture efficiency. The lipid fractions extracted from algal biomass may be converted into renewable jet fuel through hydrotreating processes, while residual biomass can support anaerobic digestion, biohydrogen generation, or thermochemical conversion. Such integrated biorefinery approaches maximize resource utilization while reducing overall environmental impact.

Synthetic biology and metabolic engineering have further accelerated the development of biological SAF production systems by enabling precise manipulation of microbial metabolic pathways [102,103]. Advances in genetic engineering have enabled researchers to design microorganisms capable of producing long-chain hydrocarbons, terpenoids, fatty alcohols, and isoprenoid-based jet fuel molecules directly from renewable carbon sources [85]. Engineered strains of cyanobacteria and yeast are being optimized for enhanced carbon fixation efficiency, improved product yields, and increased tolerance to industrial operating conditions. Metabolic pathway optimization also enables improved electron utilization, redox balancing, and carbon flux distribution during fuel synthesis [104]. These developments are critical for improving the economic viability of biological carbon conversion technologies and expanding the range of fuel molecules accessible through microbial biosynthesis [105,106].

Commercialization and large-scale deployment of CO2-derived SAF technology is principally determined by its maturity, energy demand, hydrogen availability, and economic viability [107]. Among existing pathways, biomass-based processes such as hydro-processed esters and fatty acids (HEFA) have achieved commercial maturity (TRL 9), whereas CO2-based Power-to-Liquid (PtL) and electrofuel routes remain at pilot/demonstration stages (TRL 5–7) [108]. These emerging pathways integrate renewable electricity, green hydrogen by water electrolysis, and captured CO2 through reverse water–gas shift and Fischer–Tropsch synthesis or methanol-mediated upgrading to generate drop-in jet fuels [16]. These technologies offer near-carbon-neutral fuel production, but their deployment is limited by the complexity of integrating multiple energy-intensive unit operations and maintaining continuous renewable power availability. Energy requirement of CO2-to-SAF is considerably higher than the conventional refining routes, as renewable electricity is consumed during hydrogen generation, CO2 capture, compression, and catalytic fuel synthesis [91]. Recent techno-economic analyses estimate that approximately 0.8 kg of renewable H2 and ~3.1 kg of captured CO2 are required to produce 1 kg of PtL-SAF, emphasizing the enormous demand for low-cost renewable electricity and electrolyzer capacity [108]. Consequently, the economic competitiveness of CO2-derived SAFs strongly depends on declining renewable electricity prices, improved electrolyzer efficiencies, higher carbon utilization efficiencies, and economies of scale. At present, production costs remain substantially above those of fossil-derived jet fuel, necessitating policy incentives such as carbon pricing, production tax credits, contracts for difference, and long-term airline off-take agreements to accelerate commercialization. Despite these challenges, CO2-to-SAF technologies possess significant long-term potential to produce fully compatible drop-in fuels without requiring modifications to existing aircraft or airport infrastructure. Future commercial deployment will therefore depend on expanding renewable hydrogen production, improving catalyst durability and carbon conversion efficiencies, integrating direct air capture with renewable energy systems, and establishing supportive regulatory frameworks that reduce investment risks while stimulating global SAF markets.

5.2. Electrochemical Routes to SAF

In parallel with biological systems, electrochemical carbon dioxide reduction technologies have emerged as powerful approaches for converting captured CO2 into fuel intermediates using renewable electricity [109,110]. Electrochemical reduction systems utilize electrocatalysts capable of transferring electrons to carbon dioxide molecules, thereby producing carbon monoxide, formate, methanol, methane, ethylene, ethanol, and other hydrocarbon intermediates [94,111]. Product distribution depends strongly on catalyst composition, reactor configuration, electrolyte chemistry, and operating potential [112]. Copper-based catalysts are particularly important because they can facilitate multicarbon product formation, while silver and gold catalysts exhibit high selectivity toward carbon monoxide production [113]. Formate-producing catalysts based on tin, indium, and bismuth are also attracting interest because formate serves as an important chemical intermediate and hydrogen storage medium [114]. The integration of bioelectrochemical systems with renewable energy presents a promising pathway toward circular carbon utilization, aligning aviation fuel production with long-term climate neutrality goals. Bioelectrochemical reactors enable direct electron transfer between electrodes and microorganisms, facilitating microbial electrosynthesis of fuels and chemical intermediates from carbon dioxide (Figure 7). Renewable electricity derived from solar and wind power can drive cathodic CO2 reduction while minimizing fossil energy dependence. Coupling renewable hydrogen production with microbial carbon fixation enhances fuel synthesis efficiency and enables continuous operation under variable renewable energy supply conditions [115]. Furthermore, integrating carbon capture technologies with electrochemical and biological conversion systems supports closed-loop carbon recycling by utilizing industrial emissions and atmospheric carbon as renewable feedstocks. Recent advances in nanostructured catalysts, enzyme-based electrodes, conductive biofilms, and synthetic metabolic engineering are improving conversion rates and product specificity in bioelectrochemical fuel systems. As renewable energy infrastructure expands globally, integrated carbon-neutral aviation fuel platforms may become essential components of future sustainable transportation networks, supporting both energy security and global decarbonization objectives.

Electrochemical CO2 conversion systems offer several significant advantages for SAF production. First, they operate under relatively mild temperatures and pressures compared with thermochemical processes. Second, they can be directly powered by intermittent renewable electricity generated from solar and wind sources. Third, they enable decentralized fuel production systems capable of utilizing locally captured carbon dioxide streams. Furthermore, electrochemical reactors exhibit rapid operational flexibility, making them compatible with fluctuating renewable electricity supply [112]. However, several technical challenges remain, including catalyst degradation, low energy efficiency, limited current density, and difficulties associated with downstream product separation. Significant research efforts are therefore focused on developing nanostructured catalysts, membrane electrode assemblies, gas diffusion electrodes, and advanced reactor architectures capable of improving conversion efficiency and product selectivity [85,113]. Renewable hydrogen production is another essential component of integrated carbon-to-fuel systems [81]. Hydrogen generated through renewable-powered water electrolysis acts as a reducing agent during hydrocarbon synthesis and hydro-processing operations. Green hydrogen can also be combined with captured carbon dioxide through reverse water-gas shift reactions followed by Fischer–Tropsch synthesis to generate synthetic aviation fuels [90,91].

The rapid expansion of renewable energy infrastructure has substantially improved the feasibility of hydrogen-mediated synthetic fuel pathways. Proton exchange membrane electrolysis, alkaline electrolysis, and solid oxide electrolysis technologies are increasingly being optimized for large-scale green hydrogen production. Coupling electrolysis systems with renewable electricity sources enables carbon-neutral hydrogen generation while supporting grid balancing and long-duration energy storage [5]. In integrated SAF production systems, renewable hydrogen can also enhance carbon conversion efficiency by improving hydrodeoxygenation and hydrocracking reactions during biomass upgrading.

Hybrid systems integrating biological and electrochemical processes represent a particularly promising frontier in SAF research. These systems combine the catalytic precision of biological pathways with the high electron transfer efficiency of electrochemical platforms. Microbial electrosynthesis systems, for example, utilize electroactive microorganisms capable of accepting electrons directly or indirectly from cathodes to reduce carbon dioxide into multi-carbon compounds. In such systems, renewable electricity drives cathodic reactions while microorganisms catalyze carbon fixation and product formation. This approach enables efficient coupling between renewable power generation and microbial fuel synthesis. Electroactive acetogenic bacteria can produce acetate, ethanol, and butyrate from carbon dioxide using electrons supplied through conductive surfaces or hydrogen intermediates generated electrochemically.

Bioelectrochemical systems offer several advantages compared with conventional catalytic approaches. Biological catalysts exhibit high substrate specificity and can operate under ambient conditions, reducing energy requirements and minimizing undesirable side reactions. Moreover, microorganisms possess self-regenerating catalytic capabilities that may improve long-term operational stability. Advances in electrode materials, conductive nanostructures, and biofilm engineering are improving extracellular electron transfer efficiency and enhancing microbial productivity. Carbon-based electrodes, graphene composites, conductive polymers, and metal–organic frameworks are being investigated for improving electrode biocompatibility and electron transport characteristics. These developments are expected to play a crucial role in advancing microbial electrosynthesis technologies toward industrial implementation (Table 2).

The integration of renewable energy systems with bioelectrochemical platforms is particularly important for establishing circular carbon utilization pathways aligned with long-term climate neutrality goals. Renewable electricity generated from solar photovoltaic systems, wind turbines, hydroelectric power, and bioenergy facilities can provide the electrical energy required for electrochemical carbon reduction, hydrogen generation, and microbial electrosynthesis. The intermittent nature of renewable electricity generation may also be addressed through flexible electrochemical reactor operation and hydrogen storage strategies. Excess renewable electricity generated during periods of low grid demand can be redirected toward carbon conversion systems, effectively transforming renewable power into storable liquid fuels suitable for aviation applications.

Bioenergy systems themselves can contribute significantly to renewable electricity generation and carbon management [89]. Biomass combustion, anaerobic digestion, and gasification processes produce renewable electricity and heat while generating carbon-rich gas streams suitable for capture and utilization. Integrating carbon capture technologies with biomass energy systems creates bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS) configurations capable of achieving net-negative emissions. When captured biogenic carbon dioxide is redirected toward fuel synthesis rather than permanent storage, fully circular carbon utilization pathways become possible [92]. Such systems are increasingly recognized as essential components of future carbon-neutral energy infrastructure.

Thermochemical and electrochemical integration strategies are also expanding the technological diversity of SAF production pathways [94]. Reverse water–gas shift reactors can convert captured CO2 into carbon monoxide using renewable hydrogen, thereby generating syngas suitable for Fischer–Tropsch hydrocarbon synthesis. Plasma-assisted catalysis and photocatalytic reduction systems are additionally being investigated for direct solar-driven carbon conversion [131]. Semiconductor photocatalysts capable of utilizing sunlight to drive carbon dioxide reduction reactions may eventually enable low-energy fuel synthesis systems inspired by natural photosynthesis [132]. Although these technologies remain at relatively early stages of development, they represent important directions for future sustainable fuel research.

Biological, thermochemical, and electrochemical CO2 conversion technologies are increasingly viewed as complementary components of an integrated carbon utilization framework for SAF production. Apart from possessing the individual benefits, the integration of these technologies enables each pathway to compensate for the limitations of the others. Electrochemical conversion addresses the need for renewable carbon activation, biological systems enhance product selectivity and carbon utilization while operating under low-energy conditions, and thermochemical upgrading provides the high productivity and process intensification necessary for commercial-scale fuel manufacture [82,94]. For example, electrochemically produced formate or syngas can serve as substrates for microbial fermentation, whereas biologically generated alcohols can subsequently undergo catalytic upgrading to jet-range hydrocarbons. Such hybrid platforms reduce dependence on single conversion technology, improve overall carbon efficiency, facilitate the utilization of intermittent renewable electricity, and enhance process flexibility [5,81]. Consequently, future CO2-to-SAF biorefineries are expected to integrate electrochemical, biological, and thermochemical processes into a unified value chain, leveraging the strengths of each technology to achieve greater energy efficiency, improved carbon circularity, and economically viable production of SAFs [108].

Economic feasibility remains one of the most important challenges facing carbon-to-fuel technologies. The cost of renewable electricity, green hydrogen production, carbon capture infrastructure, catalyst materials, and reactor operation currently limits large-scale commercialization of many advanced SAF pathways [133]. Nevertheless, continuous declines in renewable electricity costs, advances in electrolyzer manufacturing, and increasing carbon pricing policies are improving the economic outlook for carbon-neutral aviation fuels [134,135]. Government incentives, low-carbon fuel standards, and international aviation decarbonization mandates are expected to accelerate technology deployment during the coming decades. Lifecycle assessment and techno-economic analysis are therefore becoming increasingly important tools for evaluating the sustainability and scalability of competing SAF pathways [81,136].

Lifecycle greenhouse gas reduction remains a central criterion for SAF evaluation. Integrated carbon-to-fuel systems can potentially achieve near-net-zero or even net-negative carbon emissions depending on feedstock origin, energy source, and process integration strategy. Biomass-derived carbon recycled through biological and electrochemical pathways contributes substantially lower lifecycle emissions compared with fossil-derived jet fuels. Furthermore, the use of renewable electricity eliminates indirect emissions associated with conventional hydrogen production and fuel refining processes. However, achieving true climate neutrality requires careful consideration of land use impacts, water consumption, nutrient requirements, and infrastructure-related emissions [137]. Future SAF deployment strategies must therefore emphasize holistic sustainability assessment frameworks incorporating environmental, social, and economic dimensions [138].

Recent advances in artificial intelligence, digital process optimization, and systems engineering are also contributing to the rapid evolution of SAF technologies [118,139]. Machine learning algorithms are increasingly being applied to catalyst discovery, metabolic pathway optimization, reactor control, and process integration analysis. Digital twins and predictive modeling platforms enable real-time optimization of electrochemical reactors, biorefinery systems, and renewable energy integration strategies. Such computational tools may significantly accelerate technology development while reducing operational costs and improving process reliability [140]. The aviation industry’s transition toward sustainable fuel systems will likely require a combination of complementary technological pathways rather than reliance on a single solution. Biomass conversion, electrochemical CO2 reduction, microbial electrosynthesis, renewable hydrogen integration, and carbon capture technologies each offer distinct advantages and limitations depending on regional resource availability, infrastructure capacity, and policy frameworks. Hybrid systems integrating multiple technologies may ultimately provide the highest efficiency and flexibility for large-scale SAF deployment. For example, biological systems may be utilized for selective carbon fixation and alcohol production, while electrochemical platforms provide hydrogen generation and carbon monoxide synthesis. Thermochemical upgrading processes can subsequently convert intermediates into aviation-compatible hydrocarbons.

Integration of bioelectrochemical systems with renewable energy infrastructure therefore represents one of the most promising pathways toward circular carbon utilization and climate-neutral aviation. By transforming waste carbon dioxide into high-energy liquid fuels using renewable electricity and biological catalysis, these systems establish sustainable carbon cycles capable of reducing dependence on fossil resources. Continued advances in catalyst engineering, synthetic biology, electrochemical reactor design, renewable hydrogen production, and systems integration are expected to further improve process efficiency and economic feasibility. As global renewable energy capacity continues to expand, carbon-neutral aviation fuel production systems may become increasingly important for balancing energy supply, reducing greenhouse gas emissions, and supporting sustainable transportation networks. Ultimately, the successful implementation of carbon-to-fuel technologies will depend on coordinated collaboration among researchers, industry stakeholders, policymakers, and renewable energy developers. Strategic investments in renewable infrastructure, carbon capture systems, and advanced fuel synthesis technologies will be essential for scaling SAF production to meet future aviation demand. International climate agreements and carbon reduction policies are likely to further stimulate innovation and commercialization in this rapidly evolving field [134]. Through the integration of biological carbon fixation, electrochemical reduction, renewable electricity, and circular carbon management strategies, SAF systems have the potential to fundamentally transform the aviation industry and contribute substantially to global climate neutrality objectives.

6. Sustainability Assessment of SAF

SAF is increasingly recognized as critical near and medium-term option for reducing the climate impact of aviation. However, the term “sustainable” should not be reduced to renewable origin, technical compatibility, or life-cycle GHG reduction alone. A fuel classified as sustainable must demonstrate measurable environmental and resource-efficiency advantages across its complete value chain, including feedstock sourcing, land and water use, biomass logistics, process energy, conversion efficiency, hydrogen and electricity inputs, co-product management, fuel distribution, and final combustion. Therefore, SAF sustainability assessment requires an integrated framework combining life-cycle assessment (LCA), circular bioeconomy principles, life-cycle sustainability assessment (LCSA), resource-efficiency indicators, and multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) [141]. Recent literature has examined SAF sustainability primarily through certification and regulatory alignment, comparing frameworks like RED III and ReFuelEU Aviation with ICAO-CORSIA [141,142]. While these studies are crucial for defining feedstock eligibility, GHG limits, chain-of-custody, ILUC treatment, and policy recognition, regulatory compliance alone does not fully capture sustainability. A pathway-level assessment is needed, addressing feedstock circularity, energy intensity, hydrogen use, land-use and water risks, soil-carbon and biodiversity impacts, co-product valorization, technology readiness, and scalability. This study adopts a broader LCA and circular-bioeconomy perspective, positioning certification as a supporting governance mechanism rather than the sole basis for sustainability claims (Figure 8).

6.1. Role of Lifecycle Assessment (LCA)

LCA is one of the most widely used tools for quantifying the environmental performance of SAF. In conventional aviation fuel systems, emissions arise from crude oil extraction, transport, refining, fuel distribution, and aircraft combustion. In SAF systems, the emission profile is more pathway-specific and may include biomass cultivation or residue collection, feedstock transport, pretreatment, fermentation, gasification, hydrogenation, catalytic upgrading, electricity consumption, hydrogen production, co-product handling, blending, distribution, and final fuel use. Therefore, SAF assessment is commonly performed using well-to-wake or cradle-to-grave system boundaries, with GHG emissions expressed as g CO2-eq/MJ of fuel [143]. To facilitate comparison among different SAF production pathways, lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions are commonly reported as carbon intensity (CI) in g CO2-eq/MJ. Conventional Jet A-1 has a lifecycle carbon intensity of approximately 89 g CO2-eq/MJ, whereas representative values for major SAF pathways generally range from 15–45 g CO2-eq/MJ (HEFA), 10–35 g CO2-eq/MJ (FT), 20–55 g CO2-eq/MJ (AtJ), and <10–30 g CO2-eq/MJ (PtL), depending on feedstock, hydrogen source, electricity mix, and lifecycle boundary assumptions. A central issue in SAF LCA is the treatment of biogenic carbon. Bio-based SAF releases CO2 during combustion, but this carbon was previously absorbed from the atmosphere during biomass growth. However, this does not automatically make all bio-based SAF carbon neutral. Carbon neutrality depends on the feedstock baseline, land-use change, biomass regrowth period, soil organic carbon dynamics, fertilizer inputs, avoided decomposition, avoided burning, and alternative uses of the biomass [144]. For example, SAF derived from genuine waste oils or unavoidable residues may provide strong climate benefits, whereas SAF derived from feedstocks linked to deforestation, peatland drainage, food-crop displacement, or high fertilizer demand may have weaker or even adverse sustainability outcomes [145].

The selection of system boundaries, functional units, allocation approach, and background databases can strongly influence LCA conclusions. Most SAF studies use 1 MJ of fuel lower heating value as the functional unit, which allows comparison among fuel-production pathways. However, future aircraft-level assessments may also consider performance-based functional units, such as useful energy delivered or distance travelled, because fuel density, combustion properties, and non-CO2 effects may influence actual aviation performance. Similarly, the choice of cradle-to-gate, well-to-wake, or cradle-to-grave boundaries should be explicitly justified because excluding fuel combustion, co-product displacement, or upstream land-use effects may underestimate the real sustainability burden. Several methodological parameters require particular attention in SAF LCA. ILUC can substantially alter the carbon intensity of crop-based pathways, especially when energy crops or oil crops displace food production or trigger land conversion elsewhere [143]. Fertilizer-derived nitrous oxide emissions can also be important because N2O has high global warming potential and varies with soil type, climate, fertilizer practice, and nitrogen-use efficiency. Hydrogen source is critical for Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids (HEFA), Alcohol-to-Jet (AtJ), and other hydroprocessing-intensive routes; grey hydrogen can increase life-cycle emissions, whereas renewable hydrogen can reduce the conversion-stage footprint [145]. Carbon electricity intensity is decisive for Power-to-Liquid (PtL), electrochemical, algae, and other energy-intensive routes [87]. Co-product allocation can also significantly affect reported SAF carbon intensity because many routes produce renewable diesel, naphtha, propane, biochar, lignin-rich residues, process heat, or captured CO2. Therefore, SAF LCA studies should transparently report allocation methods and include sensitivity analysis for ILUC, fertilizer emissions, feedstock transport distance, hydrogen source, electricity mix, conversion yield, and co-product displacement [146]. Direct comparison of reported GHG reduction and carbon intensity values among SAF pathways should be made with caution, as LCA outcomes are highly dependent on methodological choices. Variations in system boundaries (e.g., cradle-to-gate, well-to-wake, or cradle-to-grave), functional units, co-product allocation methods, feedstock assumptions, hydrogen and electricity sources, and land-use change treatment can substantially influence reported results. Therefore, representative values presented in this review should be interpreted within the context of methodological assumptions of each study rather than as directly comparable performance metrics.

6.2. Pathway-Specific Sustainability Hotspots

The sustainability performance of SAF differs significantly across HEFA, Fischer–Tropsch (FT), Alcohol-to-Jet (AtJ), Sugar-to-Jet, algae-derived SAF, and Power-to-Liquid (PtL) pathways. Therefore, pathway-specific LCA hotspots must be clearly identified rather than assuming that all SAF routes provide similar benefits [147]. HEFA is among the most commercially mature routes, converting lipid feedstocks such as used cooking oil, animal fats, and vegetable oils into paraffinic hydrocarbons via hydrogenation, deoxygenation, and isomerization [148]. HEFA sustainability strongly depends on lipid origin. Waste lipids offer high circular-bioeconomy value by avoiding cultivation and reducing waste burdens. In contrast, virgin vegetable oils raise concerns over ILUC, food-versus-fuel competition, fertilizer-derived N2O emissions, biodiversity loss, and water demand. Accordingly, HEFA should be evaluated based on lipid origin, waste-oil traceability, hydrogen source, and co-product allocation.

FT-SAF relies on gasification of carbon-rich feedstocks, including agricultural residues, forest residues, and municipal solid waste (MSW), followed by syngas cleaning and catalytic synthesis. Sustainability potential is high when genuine residues are used, but biomass logistics, gasification efficiency, and carbon conversion efficiency are major LCA hotspots [87]. Excessive crop-residue removal may reduce soil organic carbon and increase erosion risk, while excessive forest-residue extraction can affect nutrient cycling. For MSW-based FT-SAF, careful sorting is required because fossil-derived plastics can increase the fossil-carbon fraction of the final fuel. Thus, residue-based FT-SAF must integrate soil-carbon protection, sustainable harvesting limits, and fossil-carbon screening [149]. AtJ-SAF converts alcohol intermediates, mainly ethanol or isobutanol, into jet-range hydrocarbons via dehydration, oligomerization, and hydrogenation. Sustainability depends heavily on the alcohol production route. Alcohols from sugar or starch feedstocks carry land-use, fertilizer, and water burdens, whereas those from lignocellulosic residues or waste gases align better with circular-bioeconomy objectives . Carbon losses during upgrading, hydrogen use, and process heat demand must also be considered.

Sugar-to-Jet pathways can be attractive when using cellulosic or industrial sugar-rich residues, but sugar-crop feedstocks raise land occupation, irrigation, and food-system concerns. Algae-derived SAF offers high productivity and CO2 utilization but faces challenges in energy-intensive harvesting, dewatering, and extraction; sustainability requires wet biomass conversion, wastewater integration, and nutrient recycling. PtL-SAF uses renewable hydrogen and captured CO2 to produce synthetic hydrocarbons, offering deep decarbonization potential without direct biomass dependence [87]. However, PtL-SAF is highly sensitive to electricity carbon intensity, electrolyzer efficiency, CO2 source, and synthesis efficiency [150]. It also requires large renewable electricity volumes, creating potential competition with other decarbonization priorities. Therefore, PtL-SAF should be assessed using prospective LCA scenarios that reflect regional grid decarbonization, electrolyzer performance, and sustainable CO2 sourcing.

6.3. Circular Bioeconomy Perspective

The circular bioeconomy concept is highly relevant to SAF because it emphasizes renewable carbon management, waste valorization, resource recovery, and reduced fossil-carbon dependence [151]. In a circular SAF system, preferred feedstocks should avoid direct competition with food production, land conversion, and ecological degradation. Suitable carbon sources include used cooking oil, animal fats, agricultural and forest residues, municipal organic waste, wastewater-grown algae, industrial off-gases, fermentation CO2, biogas-derived CO2, and renewable-energy-derived captured CO2. A waste and resource hierarchy should guide feedstock prioritization. The most preferred sources are unavoidable organic wastes, waste lipids, residues, industrial off-gases, and biogenic CO2 streams. Secondary options include cover crops or biomass grown on degraded or marginal land, provided they avoid land-use change, water stress, and food competition. Dedicated energy crops are acceptable only when regionally justified and demonstrably low-risk. First-generation food crops warrant caution due to their links to ILUC, fertilizer demand, water use, and food-versus-fuel competition [151].

However, waste or residue feedstocks do not automatically guarantee sustainability. Many residues already serve important functions: agricultural residues as soil cover or livestock bedding, forest residues in nutrient cycling, used cooking oil in biodiesel or oleochemical markets, and municipal waste as a possible source of fossil-derived plastics. Therefore, circularity must be evaluated using feedstock availability, competing uses, collection logistics, displacement effects, regional supply curves, and residue-removal limits . Cascading biomass use is another key principle. Rather than converting biomass directly to fuel in a single-use model, cascading systems extract higher-value materials first and then route the remaining residues to fuel or energy production. For example, lignocellulosic biomass may first be used for materials or biochemicals, while lignin-rich residues, black liquor, or fermentation residues can be directed to thermochemical conversion, anaerobic digestion, or energy recovery. Such integrated biorefineries can improve total resource efficiency and reduce environmental burdens assigned to SAF. Circular-bioeconomy claims should be supported by measurable indicators, including waste diversion, fossil-carbon displacement, nutrient recovery, material circularity, co-product substitution, avoided emissions, and reduced linear resource losses.

6.4. Beyond-Carbon Sustainability Indicators

Although GHG reduction drives SAF deployment, carbon intensity alone is insufficient to define sustainability. A low-carbon pathway may still create burdens related to water use, eutrophication, acidification, biodiversity loss, land occupation, toxicity, social risk, or soil degradation. Therefore, SAF assessment should include both climate and non-climate indicators [152]. For biomass-derived SAF, land-use change and soil-carbon effects are particularly important. Feedstock cultivation may require fertilizer, irrigation, and pesticides, contributing to eutrophication, ecotoxicity, water stress, and biodiversity loss. Residue-based SAF avoids direct cultivation, but excessive residue removal can reduce soil organic matter and nutrient recycling. Thus, assessment should include land-use risk, soil-carbon balance, sustainable residue-removal rates, nutrient balance, and biodiversity safeguards [143].

Water footprint is another critical indicator. Irrigated oil or sugar crops may have high water requirements, whereas waste oils, residues, wastewater-grown algae, and PtL routes may reduce agricultural water demand but introduce other burdens. Pathway-specific water use should therefore be evaluated against regional water scarcity rather than total water volume alone. A low-GHG pathway may still be unsuitable in arid regions if it increases freshwater depletion [153]. Biodiversity and ecosystem-quality indicators should also be included. Feedstocks from converted grasslands, forests, wetlands, or high-conservation-value land may generate biodiversity impacts not captured by carbon-only metrics. Residue extraction can also affect habitat quality and soil fauna if removal exceeds sustainable thresholds. Biodiversity characterization, ecosystem-service assessment, and conservation safeguards should be incorporated into future SAF LCA and LCSA studies where data permit.

Social sustainability should be considered, particularly for large-scale biomass systems and global waste supply chains. Potential risks include land-tenure conflicts, informal labor in waste collection, occupational exposure in thermochemical systems, local air-quality impacts, and unequal benefit distribution. Certification systems address some issues, but social LCA remains underused. Future studies should include labor conditions, land rights, food security, local employment, community acceptance, and occupational safety [154]. Air-quality and non-CO2 climate impacts also merit attention. Many SAFs have lower sulfur and aromatic contents than fossil jet fuel, which may reduce particulate matter and soot formation. However, non-CO2 aviation effects, including contrail and cirrus-cloud formation, depend on fuel composition, engine technology, flight altitude, and atmospheric conditions [155]. Future SAF assessments should therefore consider both CO2 and non-CO2 climate effects.

6.5. Policy, Certification, and Traceability

Policy and certification systems are essential for SAF deployment because they define eligible feedstocks, GHG accounting rules, technical certification, traceability requirements, and market access. CORSIA provides an international framework for eligible aviation fuels [143], while regional policies such as RED III and ReFuelEU Aviation impose stricter requirements for specific markets [136]. Technical certification also ensures that SAF meets aviation fuel safety, blending, and performance requirements before commercial use [142]. However, certification should be viewed as a minimum compliance mechanism rather than a complete sustainability assessment. This distinction is important because certification frameworks differ in GHG thresholds, ILUC treatment, feedstock eligibility, and traceability requirements. Recent comparative work shows that European and ICAO-CORSIA systems diverge in certification scope, chain-of-custody models, GHG accounting, and ILUC approaches [141]. Therefore, pathway-level sustainability assessment should complement certification by identifying the actual environmental hotspots and resource constraints of each SAF route. Traceability is especially critical for waste- and residue-derived SAF. As demand increases, risks of feedstock misclassification, double counting, and substitution of virgin materials for waste streams also rise. Digital traceability systems, third-party verification, mass-balance accounting, and transparent chain-of-custody documentation are therefore important for maintaining environmental integrity. Despite significant policy progress, several regulatory challenges continue to hinder large-scale SAF deployment, including differences in sustainability criteria, GHG accounting methodologies, feedstock eligibility, certification requirements, and incentive mechanisms across regions. Greater international harmonization of certification systems, transparent carbon accounting, and stable long-term policy support will be essential to accelerate global SAF commercialization and investment.

6.6. Multi-Criteria Sustainability Evaluation of SAF Pathways

Because SAF pathways involve trade-offs among climate mitigation, water use, land occupation, biodiversity, cost, scalability, technology readiness, and social safeguards, a single indicator cannot define the most sustainable option. Life-cycle sustainability assessment (LCSA) provides a broader framework by combining environmental LCA, life-cycle costing, and social LCA. This is particularly relevant for SAF because the pathway with the lowest GHG intensity may not necessarily have the lowest water footprint, biodiversity impact, cost, or social risk. Multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) can support SAF pathway ranking by integrating diverse indicators into a structured decision framework. Methods such as technique for order of preference by similarity to ideal solution (TOPSIS), Preference ranking organization method for enrichment evaluation (PROMETHEE), or weighted scoring can compare pathways using criteria including GHG reduction, water scarcity footprint, land-use risk, soil-carbon protection, feedstock circularity, social compliance, technology readiness level, production cost, scalability, and certification readiness [152]. Criterion weighting should be region-specific; for example, water scarcity may receive higher weighting in arid regions, while land-use protection may be more critical in biodiversity-sensitive or agriculturally intensive regions.

A multi-criteria approach also explains why no SAF pathway is universally sustainable. Waste-lipid HEFA may perform well where traceable waste-oil supply chains exist, but its scalability is limited by feedstock availability. Lignocellulosic FT-SAF may provide strong circularity benefits in biomass-rich regions but requires advanced conversion infrastructure and careful residue management. AtJ-SAF may be attractive where low-carbon ethanol or isobutanol is available, but its performance depends on carbon alcohol intensity and upgrading efficiency. PtL-SAF may suit regions with abundant renewable electricity and sustainable CO2 sources, although high cost and electricity demand remain key limitations. Algae-derived SAF may be promising when wastewater treatment, nutrient recovery, and CO2 utilization are integrated, but energy balance and scale-up readiness remain critical challenges [57]. Future SAF deployment should therefore be treated as a portfolio of pathways rather than a single solution. Sustainability assessment should follow a multi-layer framework covering: feedstock sourcing and circularity; conversion-stage impacts such as process energy, hydrogen source, electricity intensity, carbon efficiency, water demand, and co-product handling; broader environmental indicators including land-use change, soil carbon, eutrophication, acidification, air quality, biodiversity, and non-CO2 aviation effects; and socio-economic feasibility, including technology readiness, production cost, infrastructure compatibility, local employment, social safeguards, certification readiness, and scalability [152].

Future assessments should move beyond static carbon-intensity reporting toward dynamic, regionalized, and decision-oriented methods. Dynamic LCA can address the timing of biogenic carbon uptake and release, while regionalized LCA can improve assessment of water scarcity, land-use change, biodiversity, and soil-carbon effects [156]. Planetary-boundary-based assessment may also become important because relative GHG reduction does not guarantee absolute sustainability [157]. Overall, a credible SAF pathway should demonstrate measurable GHG reduction, responsible feedstock sourcing, low land-use and water risks, soil and biodiversity protection, transparent co-product accounting, economic feasibility, social acceptability, and compliance with recognized sustainability criteria.

Table 3 summarizes the comparative performance of the principal SAF pathways across environmental, economic, and commercialization metrics. HEFA remains the most commercially mature pathway, whereas FT and AtJ offer strong long-term scalability with continued technology development. Although PtL has the potential to achieve the lowest lifecycle carbon intensity, its deployment is currently constrained by renewable electricity and green hydrogen availability, while VFA- and algae-based pathways require further advances in product recovery, process integration, and pilot-scale validation. Despite significant advances, the commercial deployment of SAF remains constrained by high production costs, feedstock availability, renewable hydrogen demand, and capital-intensive conversion technologies. Market expansion also depends on robust supply chains, compatible infrastructure, fuel certification, and supportive policy incentives. While HEFA is commercially mature, emerging pathways such as FT, AtJ, PtL, and VFA-derived SAF require further improvements in process efficiency, cost reduction, and industrial scale-up. Therefore, integrated techno-economic assessment (TEA), life-cycle assessment (LCA), and supportive policy frameworks are essential to accelerate large-scale SAF commercialization.

7. Research Gaps and Future Perspectives

Despite significant advancements in SAF technologies, critical scientific and engineering gaps hinder large-scale commercialization. A primary challenge is the absence of feedstock-flexible production platforms capable of efficiently processing a variety of renewable carbon sources such as lignocellulosic biomass, organic wastes, algae, waste plastics, and captured CO2 within a cohesive biorefinery framework. Future research should prioritize maximizing carbon utilization efficiency over optimizing individual conversion pathways. Catalyst development is another essential area of focus. Next-generation catalysts must achieve high activity, long-term stability, resistance to coking and feedstock impurities, reduced hydrogen demand, and efficient regeneration under industrial conditions [159,160]. Additionally, process intensification through membrane-assisted separations, continuous-flow reactors, renewable hydrogen integration, AI-driven optimization, and digital twins presents opportunities to enhance energy efficiency and economic viability. Establishing standardized lifecycle assessment (LCA) and techno-economic assessment (TEA) frameworks is equally crucial for consistent comparison of SAF pathways, considering factors such as feedstock origin, hydrogen source, electricity mix, carbon efficiency, and coproduct allocation [161]. Ultimately, the future of SAF lies in integrated circular-carbon biorefineries that synergistically combine various processes, thereby maximizing renewable carbon recovery and contributing to sustainable aviation.

8. Conclusions

The future of SAF will be determined not by the availability of renewable carbon alone, but by the ability to efficiently convert diverse carbon resources into aviation-grade hydrocarbons through integrated, carbon-efficient production systems. This review demonstrates that no single pathway currently satisfies the combined requirements of feedstock availability, carbon efficiency, economic competitiveness, and industrial scalability. Instead, SAF deployment will rely on complementary technologies, each addressing different aspects of the aviation decarbonization challenge. HEFA remains the most commercially mature pathway but is constrained by sustainable lipid availability. Fischer–Tropsch (FT) synthesis provides exceptional feedstock flexibility yet requires energy-intensive gasification and high capital investment. Alcohol-to-Jet (ATJ) benefits from established fermentation platforms but suffers from carbon losses during upgrading. Lignocellulosic biorefineries maximize biomass utilization through integrated valorization of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin, whereas algae and Power-to-Liquid (PtL) technologies offer long-term carbon-neutral potential but remain limited by cultivation costs, renewable electricity demand, and hydrogen availability. Emerging volatile fatty acid (VFA)-based pathways uniquely integrate biological waste valorization with catalytic upgrading, establishing a circular-carbon route that simultaneously mitigates waste emissions and produces aviation-grade hydrocarbons.

Across all production routes, catalyst engineering has emerged as the principal determinant of carbon utilization efficiency, oxygen removal, hydrocarbon selectivity, and fuel quality. Advances in multifunctional catalysts, oxygen-vacancy engineering, and integrated biological catalytic systems have substantially improved molecular upgrading, yet common bottlenecks including feedstock heterogeneity, catalyst durability, renewable hydrogen supply, product separation, process integration, and inconsistent lifecycle assessment methodologies continue to limit commercial deployment. Future SAF development should therefore move beyond optimizing individual conversion pathways toward integrated circular-carbon biorefineries that couple biological, thermochemical, electrochemical, and catalytic technologies within a unified platform. Priorities should include feedstock-flexible processing, durable multifunctional catalysts, renewable hydrogen integration, AI-assisted process optimization, intensified product recovery, and harmonized techno-economic and lifecycle sustainability frameworks. The transition from feedstock-driven to carbon-driven integrated biorefineries represents the next paradigm in SAF development and provides the most promising pathway toward scalable, economically viable, ASTM-compliant fuels capable of supporting a resilient and net-zero aviation sector.

title: Willie Walsh: Engine OEMs Could Learn From Boeing - Aviation Week
description:
Speaking with Aviation Week’s Window Seat podcast in his last week as IATA director general, the long-time airline career executive expressed continued optimism for the global air transport industry.
Walsh, who was CEO at Aer Lingus, British Airways and International Airlines Group before becoming IATA director general in April 2021, said OEMs that have been struggling with their delivery schedules and production quality could learn from Boeing’s turnaround.
“You’ve got to give credit to Boeing under [Boeing CEO] Kelly [Ortberg] and [Boeing Commercial Airplanes CEO] Stephanie [Pope] in particular.
And I think there’s a strong lesson in that for the other OEMs,” Walsh said.
Saadia Zahidi, who is currently the managing director at the World Economic Forum, will take up the IATA role on Nov. 1, becoming the first female director general.
text:
WASHINGTON—As Willie Walsh prepares to relinquish his role as head of International Air Transport Association (IATA) to become CEO of Indian carrier IndiGo, he says the ongoing war between the U.S. and Iran is not a crisis for the airline industry but a challenge it can cope with.

Speaking with Aviation Week’s Window Seat podcast in his last week as IATA director general, the long-time airline career executive expressed continued optimism for the global air transport industry.

Walsh, who was CEO at Aer Lingus, British Airways and International Airlines Group before becoming IATA director general in April 2021, said OEMs that have been struggling with their delivery schedules and production quality could learn from Boeing’s turnaround.

“I think one of the criticisms that was leveled at Boeing going back a few years ago, when they sort of lost their way, was that they were more focused on capital markets than on serving their customers. And to be honest, I think the same could be said now of the OEMs, particularly the engine OEMs, where they have been working very hard to satisfy the market and maybe not hard enough to satisfy their customers. And for me, that’s completely unacceptable,” Walsh said.

“You’ve got to give credit to Boeing under [Boeing CEO] Kelly [Ortberg] and [Boeing Commercial Airplanes CEO] Stephanie [Pope] in particular. They’ve turned that position around and are getting great credit from the industry for the work that they’re now doing and the refocus they’ve had on their customers. And I think there’s a strong lesson in that for the other OEMs,” Walsh said.

Walsh also commented on his successor, whose appointment was announced last week. Saadia Zahidi, who is currently the managing director at the World Economic Forum, will take up the IATA role on Nov. 1, becoming the first female director general.

“Obviously, it’ll be a big change for her coming into the industry, not having experienced it before, but I think the board was very conscious when making that decision that she will have the support of the expertise within IATA. And I think it’s a strong indication of the confidence that the board has in the management structure of IATA,” he said.

Of the continued war between the U.S. and Iran, which has led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and sky-high oil and jet fuel prices, Walsh said, “The underlying demand for air travel continues to be strong. I think there is a feeling of confidence in the industry that we can steer our way through the current challenges. I don’t see this as a crisis for the industry. Clearly, we’re still forecasting profitability at an industry level. It will be very challenging for some airlines, but at an industry level, I think these are challenging times, but not crisis times.”

Walsh’s first IATA annual general meeting (AGM) as director general was in October 2021. The industry was still reeling from the impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic, but the AGM made a significant commitment to becoming carbon net zero by 2050.

Walsh was asked if that 2050 goal had been too ambitious given the continued dire lack of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) that is an important bridge to net zero. Walsh reiterated that the industry may need to reevaluate whether the 2050 net-zero target was still realistic.

“We’re at a point where I think that target is definitely in the balance. I think we can still achieve it, but it’s becoming more and more difficult every day,” Walsh told Window Seat.

“But the important point that we made at the time was that we couldn’t achieve it as airlines on our own. It would require contribution from everybody, including governments,” he said. “And it’s terrible to have to acknowledge that we’re not seeing that now. OEMs obviously haven’t played their part because they’ve been delayed in getting new aircraft into service so gross emissions are higher than they should be. We haven’t seen air traffic control reform, and that was going to be a critical part. We haven’t seen governments play their part in encouraging the production of SAF.”

Walsh noted that major oil producers could produce SAF not just for aviation but for every industry that requires a liquid fuel source, but all have walked back from earlier SAF commitments.

“There’s little incentive for them because they’re continuing to receive financial incentives to produce oil, and the incentives to produce sustainable fuels just aren’t where they should be,” Walsh added. “They really do need to come to the game and start putting some of the massive profits that they’ve made and are making today, given the current crisis with the oil supply, into a sustainable future.”

text:
A consortium of U.S. and Saudi companies is set to build a new refinery in the Persian Gulf despite the current situation in the region. The facility will have a price tag of $5 billion and a capacity of 200,000 barrels of crude oil daily, Reuters has reported.

The consortium, dubbed MERA Oil, includes Texas-based MWG Group, the Patel Family Office, and PWS, a company associated with Saudi AHQ Group. The partners are currently selecting the site of the new facility, with a short list of three possible locations from the Gulf Cooperation Council. The GCC is comprised of six Gulf states.

Besides a refinery, the project will also feature a deepwater port, storage capacity, and export facilities, the report said. The location will be outside the Strait of Hormuz, the consortium said.

At a future date, the complex may add sustainable aviation fuel processing capacity and carbon management facilities, Reuters also said in its report.

Earlier this week, Saudi Aramco had to shut down its Jazan refinery, removing 400,000 barrels daily from global refining capacity, following a strike by the Yemeni Houthis. The attack took place Saturday, and video verified by Reuters showed a large plume of smoke rising from the refinery. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group also struck Aramco facilities in Yanbu. Saudi Aramco has not commented on the damage or restart schedule. Per media reports, repairs at Jazan will take until mid-August.

The shutdown will aggravate an already rather severe supply situation in refined fuels, which analysts have been warning about for months but only began to bite in the past couple of weeks, as crack spreads soared to an all-time high due to the gap between demand for fuels and their supply amid fighting in the Persian Gulf, the Red Sea, and Russia. On the good news side, Russia has begun restarting refineries damaged by Ukrainian drone strikes. On the bad news side, its ban on diesel exports is still in place.

text:
On 23rd July the first A350-1000ULR flight test aircraft MSN707 embarked on its longest point-to-point flight from Toulouse direct to Melbourne, Australia. Then a few days later it flew all the way back with two Qantas guest pilots on board, landing in Toulouse on the morning of July 28th. To find out more about this impressive undertaking, we sat down with Airbus Test Pilot, Xavier Pepin, who captained the aircraft on its longest ever flight - covering a distance of 12,460nm in a flight time of 24 hours and 24 minutes!

Aims of the long range flights with MSN707

This flight-test aircraft, MSN707, which first flew on the 2nd June is equipped with specialised instrumentation and is now really ‘stretching its legs’ for the first time. Its two-part voyage is technically classified as a ‘development’ flight test (as distinct from a ‘certification’ flight test).

The goal is to demonstrate that the aircraft, powered by two Rolls-Royce Trent XWB-97 engines, can perform a 23-hour ‘block time’ flight. This is the duration from releasing the parking brake at departure to setting it at the arrival stand – to ensure coverage for the customer’s intended 21 hours 40 minutes flight time (plus holding, diversion and taxi times at departure and arrival), for its forthcoming “Project Sunrise” routes.

In particular, the mission also serves to validate cabin comfort through air conditioning (ATA Chapter 21) measurements and fuel management systems (ATA Chapter 28), particularly the additional rear center tank (RCT) – with a 20,900 litre fuel capacity – which enables ultra-long-range (ULR) flights to cover a distance of almost 10,000 nm.

Xavier explains: “Whilst we have already demonstrated much of the RCT’s functionality earlier in the flight test campaign, we finalised some remaining test points in these long range flights. So we filled this tank to validate all necessary parameters during the mission, making this, along with cabin comfort, the primary focus of our testing.”

He adds: “During the first leg we also made use of the time (the flight lasted approximately 20 hours) to stabilise various air temperature settings to ensure accurate measurements. So while much of the testing goals were already tackled on the outward leg, the second leg addressed any backup test points that were not completed during the first leg.”

Furthermore, the crew evaluated the ULR’s new twin Flight Crew Rest Compartment (FCRC) – which was extensively instrumented to measure the air conditioning performance. This new module, specially designed for the -1000ULR’s ultra long missions, features two separate, dedicated sections with individual entrances. This modification ensures that in airline operation pilots can enter or exit their respective rest areas without disturbing one another.

Flight crew roster and routing aspects

For the outward leg there were four Airbus pilots, with Test Pilot, Vincent Sibelle, as captain (and also being responsible / in-charge of the overall mission organisation). The other three pilots on board were Xavier Pepin, Josef Bayoud and Chetan Takalkar. In addition to these pilots, the crew included two Test-Flight Engineers (TFEs), Laurent Rossignol and Nicolas Granier, who were seated in the cockpit to monitor aircraft systems and three Flight-Test Engineers (FTEs), Tuan Do, Alexia Plumet and Jaime Angoloti, who were seated at their flight test work stations (in the main cabin) to coordinate all tests including cabin comfort and fuel monitoring.

For the return leg – from Melbourne back to Toulouse – Airbus Test Pilot, Xavier Pepin, was designated as captain. Moreover, for this leg two Qantas pilots Captain Andrew Coull and Captain David Summergreene joined the crew and one of the Airbus pilots disembarked. So all in all, on the return flight there were five pilots on board – comprising three Airbus pilots plus the two Qantas pilots who are already qualified on the A350 but who were new to the ULR variant. Meanwhile, the two TFEs and three FTE’s were the same as for the outward flight.

This even longer flight involved taking off from Melbourne, crossing the Pacific toward Los Angeles, traversing the US and Canada, and then crossing the Atlantic south of Greenland, then over the UK and back to southern France.

Xavier explained that for the return flight a northerly Atlantic path was chosen to avoid the published tracks in use by airlines that might not be updated by the time of takeoff, thereby avoiding potential Air Traffic Control (ATC) issues, such as mis-matching flight plans.

Fatigue management and crew rest during the flight

Xavier recalls: “To manage fatigue during the 20 to 23-hour flights we implemented four-hour shifts for each pilot, but we rotated the crew every two hours. This staggered approach ensures that when a new pilot joins the cockpit, they overlap for two hours with the outgoing pilot. This facilitates a thorough handover and maintains full situational awareness. Additionally, for the second flight leg, at least one Airbus test pilot was always seated in a pilot seat when a Qantas pilot was in the other seat to ensure mission safety, as Airbus holds responsibility for the operation. We have applied this same structure to manage rest periods effectively.”

Notably, because the aircraft’s new ‘twin’ flight crew rest compartments were ‘occupied’ with ventilation measurement equipment, the crew used instead the eight-berth cabin crew rest compartment at the rear of the aircraft for their sleep.

“In the rear cabin crew rest compartment, since there weren’t any passengers or cabin crew, we could quickly return to the cockpit or FTE station at any time if needed,” notes Xavier.

“We have organised a schedule to allow a Qantas pilot to take the controls at specific times. These pilots are already qualified on the A350, and this mission provided them with their first experience with the -1000ULR variant.”

“We really enjoyed and appreciated exchanging knowledge and addressing their questions during our ultra-long-range voyage together,” he concludes.

text:
A new report from Clean Air Task Force (CATF) finds that directing sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) to a small number of high-impact airports, rather than spreading it across the aviation network, could significantly increase the fuel’s climate and public health benefits while global supply continues to build. The report, Maximizing the Climate Co-Benefits of Sustainable Aviation Fuel via Targeted Allocation, analyzed 2024 flight activity at major U.S. and European airports to identify where targeted SAF use would have the biggest impact.

“Every ton of SAF reduces carbon emissions no matter where it’s used, but that’s not true of the fuel’s other climate and health benefits,” said Thomas Walker, Associate Director for Transportation Technology at Clean Air Task Force and a co-author of the report. “Contrail formation and local air pollution are both highly dependent on where and when a plane takes off. That means a relatively small amount of SAF, directed to the right airports, could do far more good than the same amount spread evenly across the system – especially while SAF supplies are highly limited.”

Working with aviation climate data company Estuaire, CATF analyzed 16.6 million flights at major U.S. and European airports in 2024, examining contrail formation as well as particulate matter and nitrogen oxide emissions during landing and takeoff. The analysis found that just 2% of flights generate 80% of contrail-related warming, meaning a targeted approach can capture most of the climate benefit without requiring a large share of the global SAF supply, which made up just 0.7% of the jet fuel market in 2025.

Based on a combination of contrail impacts and air quality benefits, the report identifies John F. Kennedy International Airport, Los Angeles International Airport, and O’Hare International Airport as priority U.S. locations for targeted SAF allocation. In Europe, London Heathrow, Istanbul Airport, and Paris Charles de Gaulle were identified for the same reasons. JFK and Heathrow stand out as both operating large numbers of long-haul, internationally distributed flights that regularly cross ice-supersaturated regions over the North Atlantic, where contrails form most readily.

The report models the effect of blending SAF at these six airports at rates from 10% to 100%. At a 50% blend, contrail-related warming fell by 30% to 34% at the U.S. airports studied and 33% to 40% at the European airports, while particulate emissions during landing and takeoff dropped 26% to 28% at all six locations.

“The health benefits alone make a strong case for targeting,” said Lucía M. Maroto, Transportation Decarbonization Manager for Europe at CATF and a co-author of the report. “Our analysis shows that targeted SAF use could reduce particulate pollution around major airports, helping to limit exposure in the communities most directly affected by aviation’s air-quality impacts. Given that baseline air-pollution mortality in Europe runs two to three times higher than in the U.S., the public health case for targeting major hubs such as Paris Charles de Gaulle and Heathrow is particularly strong.”

The report also examined more targeted strategies, finding that concentrating SAF use during winter months or evening and overnight departures, when contrail formation is most common, delivers more climate benefit per ton of fuel than blending it evenly across all flights at an airport. London Heathrow is already pursuing a version of this approach: the airport uplifted 17% of the world’s available SAF supply in 2024 and is working to double that volume in 2026.

The report’s authors caution that targeting SAF to specific airports or flights introduces real logistical complexity, since much of the existing fuel supply infrastructure, particularly airports served by shared pipeline networks, was not designed to support differentiated blending. To address this, the report recommends that policymakers explicitly recognize contrail and air quality effects in aviation policy, fund further research into targeting strategies, and support pilot programs at high-impact airports to test targeted SAF deployment under real operating conditions.

title: Maximizing the Climate Co-Benefits of Sustainable Aviation Fuel via Targeted Allocation
description:
Mitigating the health and climate impact of the aviation sector will be particularly challenging as success involves transitioning to sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), which at present is more expensive than conventional jet fuel and not produced at a scale that can affect the entire market.
Sustainable aviation fuel will remain scarce and expensive for years, so where it’s used can matter as much as how much of it is used.
Targeting available SAF to a small number of high-impact airports can maximize climate and public health benefits well before SAF supply scales to meet total aviation fuel demand.
Clean Air Task Force, in partnership with the aviation climate data company Estuaire, analyzed 2024 flight activity at major U.S. and European airports to identify where targeted SAF use would have the biggest impact.
The analysis finds that directing sustainable aviation fuel to a small number of high-impact airports, rather than spreading it across the aviation network, could significantly increase the fuel’s climate and public health benefits while global supply continues to build.

As far as India is concerned, our impacts are not as dramatic," he told ANI, adding that "there are a lot of airspace restrictions in the world. It means longer flight times, it means higher cost. We all hope that this issue is resolved as soon as possible." Markette was speaking on the sidelines of the Travel Destination Germany Press Conference 2026 in New Delhi, where Lufthansa Group highlighted Germany's tourism potential and its plans to strengthen tourism and business ties with India. He said India remains a key strategic market for the airline and that the group is focused on making travel for Indian passengers more seamless, comfortable and convenient. "We have a number of expansions that we're looking at in terms of flight frequencies, bringing bigger aircraft, bringing newer aircraft. We are upgrading our Mumbai-Munich flight to an A380. We will be launching a brand new flight from Zurich to Bangalore at the end of October, and expansion will continue as we go," he said. On Lufthansa's partnership with Air India, Markette said the collaboration was in progress. "It's progressing very healthily. I can't really say much more than that, but we are working on common objectives, and I'm confident that it will be successful," he said. Markette said the Indian aviation sector is witnessing exciting growth and that Lufthansa Group is keen to be part of the country's aviation expansion. On Lufthansa's business plans in India, he said the airline would continue to increase capacity, introduce new products and expand its presence, but declined to disclose financial projections for the current fiscal year. I can tell you that overall we are expanding our presence, we are growing the number of seats, we are bringing our new products, and we are making the Lufthansa Group more accessible and more attractive to our Indian customers," he said. "Lufthansa does hedge our jet fuel. So to an extent we are hedged, meaning somewhat protected from these price increases. But clearly the jet fuel prices are a significant impact on the industry, and they will continue to have an impact," he said. He added that fuel price volatility extends beyond aviation. "Increasing oil prices do not only affect our industry, but they affect the price of a loaf of bread as well," he said, adding that while Lufthansa does not buy fuel on a day-to-day basis because of hedging arrangements, rising prices continue to pose a challenge for airlines. FutureMetrics LLC has published a new white paper that discusses the potential for using torrefied pellets as feedstock in Fischer-Tropsch (FT) gasification systems to produce sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

SAF demand is expected to grow exponentially in the future, from approximately 2 or 3 million metric tons currently to more than 40 million metric tons in 2035. Currently, most SAF is produced via the HEFA process from renewable oil feedstocks, such as soybean oil, used cooking oil, and animal fats.

In the whitepaper, authors William Struass and Laurenz Schmidt, explain that the expected explosive growth in SAF production will require additional types of feedstocks, including residues form the forest products industry.

FT technology provides a method to convert woody biomass into SAF. “The SAF refinery needs consistent feedstock, and prefers feedstock that has high C, low moisture, and low levels of minerals (ash),” Strauss and Schmidt wrote. “Delivering the highest carbon content and least unwanted non-carbon components, within technical and economic constraints, will improve the SAF output per tonne of input, and it will lower operating costs.

“Doing that with biomass requires specific expertise and experience,” they continued. “SAF refinery operators are not likely to have that expertise.”

Aeroporti di Roma (ADR), part of the Mundys Group, has inaugurated Open – FCO Smart Workplace, a new office complex at Rome Fiumicino Airport (FCO) designed to support airlines, airport operators and businesses while reinforcing the airport’s position as one of Europe’s leading aviation hubs.

Located opposite Terminal 1, the 16,000m² development expands the airport’s commercial infrastructure and forms part of ADR’s long-term strategy to strengthen the airport’s role as an integrated business and transport hub. The facility is expected to accommodate up to 600 people across 70 offices and 35 meeting rooms.

Several airlines, including ITA Airways, Emirates, American Airlines, Alaska Air, Delta Air Lines and Air Canada, will relocate office operations into the new building, alongside ground handling companies and car rental providers operating at the airport.

Smart workplace supports future airport growth

Designed to provide flexible working environments, the complex includes modular office space, shared work areas, conference facilities and dedicated spaces for meetings, workshops and corporate events. While developed primarily for the aviation sector, ADR said the facility will also be available to businesses seeking meeting and networking space close to the airport.

The building has been designed to achieve LEED certification and incorporates a range of sustainability measures. These include low-impact construction materials, façades designed to reduce solar heat gain, a 67kWp photovoltaic system, low-energy LED lighting, a Building Management System to monitor energy consumption and space utilisation, and a dual water network that enables industrial water to be used for building services.

During construction, artificial intelligence-powered video surveillance technology was deployed to improve safety by monitoring work activities and identifying unauthorised access or failures to use personal protective equipment.

The inauguration also featured the unveiling of Continuum, a site-specific artwork by Italian artist Michela Picchi, reflecting ADR’s wider commitment to integrating art and culture throughout the passenger and workplace environment.

Marco Troncone, Chief Executive Officer of Aeroporti di Roma, said: “With OPEN, we are taking another step forward in the development of our airport, creating an innovative and sustainable facility that strengthens our office offering, as well as Rome Fiumicino’s ability to serve as an integrated hub for the entire airport industrial district, operators, airlines and businesses.

“OPEN represents a new chapter in our growth strategy towards the airport of the future, which looks at accommodating 100 million passengers by 2046, further consolidating Fiumicino’s role as a global, innovative and sustainable airport.”

More than 80 regional and international stakeholders gathered at the ISCC Regional Stakeholder Committee Latin America conference to discuss circular economy policy, alternative feedstocks, sustainable fuels and certification as the region expands its role in low-carbon industries.

The event opened with presentations outlining Mexico's circular economy strategy and the country's evolving climate commitments. Officials highlighted Mexico's latest Nationally Determined Contribution under the Paris Agreement, which identifies the circular economy as a key strategy for reducing emissions. The country's proposed General Circular Economy Law was presented as a framework designed to connect environmental and industrial policy while strengthening governance, regulatory certainty and extended producer responsibility.

ISCC representatives also provided updates on the certification system's growth across Latin America, noting increased adoption as sustainability regulations and market expectations continue to evolve. The organization highlighted expanding opportunities in sustainable aviation fuel and maritime fuel markets, along with new tools intended to support compliance with the European Union Deforestation Regulation and regenerative agriculture initiatives.

A series of technical presentations focused on alternative feedstocks and sustainable fuels. Clean hydrogen also received significant attention during the conference. Industry representatives described rapid growth in hydrogen projects worldwide while pointing to Latin America's potential to attract investment.
